rationale: The mother is RhD-negative, has a history of a previous RhD-positive pregnancy without anti-D prophylaxis, and now has rising anti-D antibodies. Raised fetal middle cerebral artery velocity suggests fetal anaemia, and hydrops features support severe haemolytic disease of the fetus. ABO incompatibility typically causes neonatal jaundice rather than severe antenatal hydrops. Parvovirus B19 can cause fetal anaemia but the anti-D history is the key discriminator. Twin-to-twin transfusion requires a monochorionic twin pregnancy. Alpha-thalassaemia major can cause hydrops but is not suggested by the maternal antibody findings.
clinical_context: In UK antenatal care, blood group and antibody screening are performed at booking and again later in pregnancy to identify clinically significant red cell antibodies.
simplified_explanation: The mother has made antibodies against RhD-positive fetal red cells. These antibodies cross the placenta and destroy fetal red blood cells, causing anaemia and swelling of the fetus.
guideline_anchor: NICE antenatal care and British Society for Haematology principles on red cell antibodies in pregnancy
exam_tip: Raised fetal MCA velocity in an alloimmunised pregnancy points to fetal anaemia.
tested_concept: Recognition of haemolytic disease of the fetus from maternal anti-D sensitisation
learning_objective: Identify RhD alloimmunisation as a cause of fetal anaemia and hydrops in pregnancy.

rationale: The combination of chorea, cognitive and psychiatric features, autosomal dominant family history and onset in mid-adulthood is typical of Huntington's disease. Diagnosis is confirmed by genetic testing for an expanded CAG repeat in the HTT gene, with appropriate counselling and consent. MRI may show caudate atrophy but is not definitive. Caeruloplasmin is used in suspected Wilson's disease. EEG and CSF oligoclonal bands do not confirm Huntington's disease.
clinical_context: In UK practice, diagnostic and predictive testing for Huntington's disease should involve genetic counselling because results have implications for the patient and relatives.
simplified_explanation: Huntington's disease is caused by a specific repeated DNA sequence in the HTT gene. A blood genetic test can confirm it.
guideline_anchor: standard UK clinical genetics practice
exam_tip: Chorea plus autosomal dominant family history: confirm with HTT CAG repeat testing.
tested_concept: Confirmatory genetic testing for Huntington's disease
learning_objective: Select HTT gene CAG repeat testing as the confirmatory investigation for suspected Huntington's disease.

rationale: A febrile convulsion occurs in a child aged 6 months to 5 years with fever and no evidence of CNS infection. This seizure was focal, involving the left arm and face, so it is classified as complex even though it lasted less than 15 minutes. A simple febrile convulsion is generalised, lasts less than 15 minutes and does not recur within 24 hours. Absence seizures are brief episodes of impaired awareness without fever or prolonged postictal drowsiness. Rigors are shaking without loss of consciousness or epileptic features. Breath-holding attacks are typically triggered by crying or distress.
clinical_context: Febrile convulsions are common in young children; assessment focuses on identifying the source of fever and excluding meningitis or encephalitis.
simplified_explanation: A fever-related seizure is called complex if it is one-sided, lasts more than 15 minutes, or happens more than once in the same illness.
guideline_anchor: NICE guidance on fever in under 5s and standard UK paediatric practice
exam_tip: Focal, prolonged or recurrent febrile seizure equals complex febrile convulsion.
tested_concept: Distinguishing complex from simple febrile convulsions
learning_objective: Recognise focal features as a criterion for complex febrile convulsion.

rationale: Sudden severe pain out of proportion to examination findings in a patient with atrial fibrillation and raised lactate is highly suggestive of acute mesenteric ischaemia. In a stable patient without peritonitis, CT angiography with intravenous contrast is the investigation most likely to confirm the diagnosis and identify arterial or venous occlusion. Flexible sigmoidoscopy is more useful for distal colitis and is not adequate for acute mesenteric ischaemia. Doppler ultrasound is operator-dependent and less reliable acutely. Plain radiographs are insensitive. Non-contrast CT may miss vascular occlusion and bowel enhancement abnormalities.
clinical_context: Acute mesenteric ischaemia is a surgical and radiological emergency; early CT angiography helps guide revascularisation or operative management.
simplified_explanation: The bowel may be losing its blood supply. A contrast CT timed to show the blood vessels is the best test when the patient is stable enough for imaging.
guideline_anchor: standard UK emergency surgical and radiology practice
exam_tip: Pain out of proportion plus AF: think embolic mesenteric ischaemia and request CT angiography.
tested_concept: Investigation of suspected acute mesenteric ischaemia
learning_objective: Choose CT angiography as the key diagnostic test for suspected acute mesenteric ischaemia in a stable patient.

rationale: ME/CFS is a clinical diagnosis supported by typical symptoms and exclusion of other causes. NICE recommends considering baseline tests such as FBC, U&Es, LFTs, thyroid function, ESR or plasma viscosity, CRP, calcium/phosphate, HbA1c, ferritin, coeliac screening, CK and urinalysis as clinically appropriate. MRI, polysomnography and viral serology are not routine unless suggested by specific features. It is inappropriate to make the diagnosis without considering common alternative causes such as anaemia, thyroid disease, diabetes, inflammatory disease and coeliac disease.
clinical_context: In primary care, patients with persistent fatigue should be assessed for ME/CFS features while also checking for common treatable conditions.
simplified_explanation: ME/CFS cannot be confirmed by one test. Basic blood tests help make sure a common medical problem is not causing the fatigue.
guideline_anchor: NICE guideline on myalgic encephalomyelitis/chronic fatigue syndrome
exam_tip: ME/CFS is clinical, but first exclude common mimics with targeted baseline tests.
tested_concept: Baseline investigations to exclude alternative causes of chronic fatigue
learning_objective: Select appropriate initial tests when considering ME/CFS and avoid over-investigation without clinical indication.

rationale: Echocardiography estimates the probability of pulmonary hypertension, but confirmation requires right heart catheterisation to directly measure pulmonary artery pressures and haemodynamics. High-resolution CT and V/Q scanning may help identify causes such as interstitial lung disease or chronic thromboembolic disease. Cardiac MRI can assess right ventricular structure and function but does not replace haemodynamic confirmation. Peak flow monitoring is not relevant.
clinical_context: Patients with suspected pulmonary hypertension are usually referred to a specialist pulmonary hypertension centre for confirmation and classification before disease-specific therapy.
simplified_explanation: An echo can suggest high pressure in the lung arteries, but a catheter test directly measures the pressure and confirms the diagnosis.
guideline_anchor: NICE and UK specialist pulmonary hypertension service principles
exam_tip: Echo screens; right heart catheterisation confirms pulmonary hypertension.
tested_concept: Confirmatory testing for pulmonary hypertension
learning_objective: Identify right heart catheterisation as the definitive test for confirming pulmonary hypertension.

rationale: CT-confirmed subarachnoid haemorrhage requires urgent specialist discussion for vascular imaging, aneurysm securing and neurocritical care planning. Lumbar puncture is not needed when CT has already confirmed the diagnosis. Anticoagulation would increase bleeding risk. Observation or outpatient follow-up would be unsafe because of risks of rebleeding, hydrocephalus and vasospasm.
clinical_context: In UK practice, patients with confirmed spontaneous subarachnoid haemorrhage are managed via regional neurosurgical or neurovascular pathways.
simplified_explanation: Bleeding around the brain can rebleed and may be due to an aneurysm. The patient needs urgent specialist care to find and treat the source.
guideline_anchor: NICE guidance on subarachnoid haemorrhage caused by a ruptured aneurysm
exam_tip: Once SAH is confirmed, do not do LP; urgently involve neurosurgery or the neurovascular centre.
tested_concept: Initial management pathway after CT-confirmed subarachnoid haemorrhage
learning_objective: Recognise the need for urgent specialist neurosurgical or neurovascular referral after confirmed subarachnoid haemorrhage.

rationale: This patient has rhabdomyolysis with acute kidney injury and life-threatening hyperkalaemia causing ECG changes. The immediate priority is myocardial membrane stabilisation with intravenous calcium gluconate, followed by measures to shift and remove potassium and aggressive intravenous fluid resuscitation. IV fluids are essential in rhabdomyolysis but do not address the immediate arrhythmia risk. Furosemide is not first-line for forced diuresis and may worsen hypovolaemia. Routine urine alkalinisation is not the immediate priority. Outpatient monitoring would be unsafe.
clinical_context: Rhabdomyolysis in emergency care is treated with early fluids, monitoring for compartment syndrome and urgent correction of dangerous electrolyte abnormalities.
simplified_explanation: Muscle breakdown has released potassium into the blood. Because the ECG shows the heart is at risk, calcium must be given immediately to protect it.
guideline_anchor: Resus Council UK and standard UK emergency hyperkalaemia management principles
exam_tip: In rhabdomyolysis, ECG changes from hyperkalaemia make IV calcium the first immediate step.
tested_concept: Prioritising emergency treatment of life-threatening hyperkalaemia in rhabdomyolysis
learning_objective: Manage rhabdomyolysis complicated by ECG changes from severe hyperkalaemia by giving immediate intravenous calcium.

rationale: Adult-onset Still's disease is characterised by high spiking fevers, evanescent salmon-pink rash, sore throat, arthralgia or arthritis, neutrophilic leucocytosis and markedly raised ferritin. Negative ANA and rheumatoid factor support the diagnosis. SLE is less likely with neutrophilia and negative ANA. Endocarditis can cause prolonged fever but does not typically cause the salmon rash and extreme ferritin pattern, and cultures are negative. Hodgkin lymphoma can cause fever but the rash, sore throat and inflammatory pattern are more typical of Still's disease. Subacute thyroiditis would usually cause neck pain and thyrotoxic features.
clinical_context: Pyrexia of unknown origin requires systematic assessment for infection, malignancy, inflammatory disease and drug-related causes.
simplified_explanation: This pattern of daily high fevers, joint pains, a salmon-coloured rash and extremely high ferritin is classic for adult-onset Still's disease.
guideline_anchor: standard UK clinical practice for pyrexia of unknown origin assessment
exam_tip: Very high ferritin plus quotidian fever and salmon-pink rash suggests adult-onset Still's disease.
tested_concept: Recognition of adult-onset Still's disease as a cause of pyrexia of unknown origin
learning_objective: Identify adult-onset Still's disease from quotidian fever, evanescent rash, arthralgia, neutrophilia and very high ferritin.

rationale: The flare risk is 50% with standard care and 30% with the intervention. The absolute risk reduction is 20%, or 0.20. NNT is 1 divided by absolute risk reduction: 1/0.20 = 5. The other options result from using relative rather than absolute differences or incorrect arithmetic.
clinical_context: Eczema treatments are often assessed by reductions in flares, symptom scores or need for topical corticosteroids; NNT helps interpret the clinical usefulness of an intervention.
simplified_explanation: The programme prevents flares in 20 extra children out of every 100 treated. That means treating 5 children prevents 1 flare.
guideline_anchor: standard UK clinical epidemiology principles
exam_tip: NNT = 1 / absolute risk reduction; use proportions, not percentages.
tested_concept: Calculating number needed to treat from absolute risk reduction
learning_objective: Calculate NNT using event rates from a clinical trial.

rationale: The best answer is calcium pyrophosphate crystal arthritis, commonly called pseudogout. It classically affects older adults and often presents as an acute monoarthritis of the knee. Chondrocalcinosis and rhomboid-shaped weakly positively birefringent crystals are characteristic. Gout usually causes needle-shaped negatively birefringent monosodium urate crystals and commonly affects the first metatarsophalangeal joint. Septic arthritis must always be considered in an acute hot joint, but the crystal findings and absence of systemic features make CPPD the best diagnosis here. Reactive arthritis usually follows gastrointestinal or genitourinary infection and is typically an asymmetric oligoarthritis. Osteoarthritis flare would not explain crystal findings.
clinical_context: In UK practice, acute monoarthritis should be assessed urgently, and joint aspiration is important to distinguish crystal arthritis from infection.
simplified_explanation: Pseudogout often affects the knee in older people. The key clues are calcium deposits on X-ray and rhomboid crystals that are positively birefringent.
guideline_anchor: standard UK clinical practice
exam_tip: Needle-shaped negative crystals suggest gout; rhomboid positive crystals suggest CPPD.
tested_concept: Recognition of calcium pyrophosphate crystal arthritis from synovial fluid and radiographic findings
learning_objective: Identify pseudogout as an acute crystal arthritis associated with chondrocalcinosis and positively birefringent rhomboid crystals.

rationale: Hypokalaemia with hypertension and metabolic alkalosis in a patient not taking diuretics suggests mineralocorticoid excess, most commonly primary hyperaldosteronism. The appropriate screening investigation is the plasma aldosterone:renin ratio. A short Synacthen test investigates adrenal insufficiency, which more typically causes hyperkalaemia and hypotension. A 24-hour urinary free cortisol may be used when Cushing syndrome is suspected, but the stem does not describe typical features. Urinary catecholamines are used for suspected phaeochromocytoma, usually with episodic headache, sweating and palpitations. Serum magnesium may contribute to refractory hypokalaemia but would not explain hypertension with alkalosis as well as hyperaldosteronism.
clinical_context: Primary hyperaldosteronism is an important potentially treatable cause of secondary hypertension in UK practice.
simplified_explanation: Low potassium plus high blood pressure suggests too much aldosterone. The screening test compares aldosterone with renin.
guideline_anchor: NICE hypertension guidance and standard UK endocrine practice
exam_tip: Think primary aldosteronism when hypertension is paired with unexplained hypokalaemia.
tested_concept: Investigating hypokalaemia with hypertension due to suspected primary hyperaldosteronism
learning_objective: Select aldosterone:renin ratio as the appropriate screening test for suspected primary hyperaldosteronism.

rationale: This patient has dysfunction of multiple organ systems following sepsis: renal failure with oliguria and raised creatinine, respiratory failure requiring high-flow oxygen, hepatic dysfunction with raised bilirubin, haematological dysfunction with thrombocytopenia, neurological impairment and raised lactate indicating tissue hypoperfusion. This pattern is most consistent with multi-organ dysfunction syndrome. Hepatic encephalopathy would not explain the renal, respiratory and haematological abnormalities. Acute kidney injury alone is too narrow. Disseminated intravascular coagulation can occur in sepsis and may contribute to thrombocytopenia, but the clinical picture is broader than coagulation failure alone. Opioid toxicity causes reduced consciousness and respiratory depression but does not explain progressive organ failure and high lactate.
clinical_context: In palliative and acute hospital settings, recognising multi-organ dysfunction helps guide escalation discussions, treatment goals and communication with patients and families.
simplified_explanation: Severe infection can cause several organs to fail at the same time, such as kidneys, lungs, liver, brain and blood clotting systems.
guideline_anchor: NICE sepsis guidance and standard UK palliative care principles
exam_tip: MODS is suggested by simultaneous deterioration in several organ systems after a major insult such as sepsis.
tested_concept: Recognition of multi-organ dysfunction syndrome in severe sepsis and advanced illness
learning_objective: Identify multi-organ dysfunction syndrome when infection is followed by failure of several organ systems.

rationale: A small sliding hiatus hernia commonly causes gastro-oesophageal reflux symptoms. In the absence of alarm features, initial management is lifestyle advice, such as weight reduction if appropriate, avoiding late meals and elevating the head of the bed, plus a proton pump inhibitor trial. Urgent surgery is not first-line for uncomplicated symptoms. Metoclopramide is not recommended as long-term first-line treatment because of adverse effects. Oesophageal manometry is usually reserved for selected patients before anti-reflux surgery or when motility disorders are suspected. H. pylori eradication should not be given without appropriate testing and is not the main treatment for reflux due to hiatus hernia.
clinical_context: Most sliding hiatus hernias in UK practice are managed medically unless symptoms are refractory or complications occur.
simplified_explanation: A sliding hiatus hernia often causes reflux. The usual first treatment is reflux lifestyle advice and a PPI such as omeprazole.
guideline_anchor: NICE gastro-oesophageal reflux disease and dyspepsia guidance
exam_tip: Uncomplicated sliding hiatus hernia is usually treated like GORD first.
tested_concept: Initial management of symptomatic sliding hiatus hernia with reflux symptoms
learning_objective: Manage uncomplicated reflux symptoms from a sliding hiatus hernia with lifestyle measures and acid suppression.

rationale: Severe pain out of proportion, rapidly spreading erythema, dusky skin, crepitus and septic shock after surgery are concerning for necrotising soft tissue infection involving the surgical site. The priority is urgent senior surgical involvement, resuscitation, broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotics and emergency debridement for source control. Removing clips and observing is unsafe. CT may help in uncertain stable cases, but imaging must not delay surgery in a shocked patient with clear clinical features. Oral antibiotics are inadequate. Negative pressure wound therapy may be used later after debridement and infection control, not as initial management.
clinical_context: Postoperative necrotising infection is uncommon but time-critical; early operative source control is central to survival.
simplified_explanation: A rapidly worsening painful infected wound with shock and gas under the skin needs emergency surgery and IV antibiotics.
guideline_anchor: NICE sepsis guidance and standard UK surgical infection practice
exam_tip: Pain out of proportion plus systemic toxicity after surgery should make you think of necrotising infection.
tested_concept: Management of severe postoperative wound infection with features of necrotising soft tissue infection
learning_objective: Recognise severe surgical site infection requiring immediate resuscitation, broad-spectrum antibiotics and urgent operative source control.

rationale: Progressive unilateral sensorineural hearing loss, unilateral tinnitus and imbalance are typical of vestibular schwannoma. The reduced corneal reflex suggests trigeminal nerve involvement from a cerebellopontine angle lesion, supporting this diagnosis. Ménière disease causes episodic vertigo with fluctuating hearing loss, tinnitus and aural fullness rather than progressive cranial nerve signs. Otosclerosis causes conductive hearing loss, so Rinne would usually be negative on the affected side and Weber would lateralise to the affected ear. Benign paroxysmal positional vertigo causes brief positional vertigo without hearing loss. Cholesteatoma usually has abnormal otoscopy and conductive hearing loss.
clinical_context: In UK ENT practice, unilateral sensorineural hearing loss with tinnitus is an important red flag for MRI internal auditory meatus assessment.
simplified_explanation: A vestibular schwannoma is a benign tumour on the hearing and balance nerve. It causes one-sided hearing loss, tinnitus and balance problems, and can affect nearby nerves.
guideline_anchor: NICE hearing loss in adults guidance
exam_tip: Unilateral sensorineural hearing loss plus tinnitus should prompt consideration of vestibular schwannoma.
tested_concept: Recognition of vestibular schwannoma from unilateral sensorineural hearing loss with cranial nerve involvement
learning_objective: Identify vestibular schwannoma as a cause of progressive unilateral sensorineural hearing loss, tinnitus, imbalance and trigeminal involvement.

rationale: An unexplained fracture in a non-mobile infant, inconsistent history and bruising of different ages are highly concerning for non-accidental injury. The child should be kept safe, admitted if needed, discussed urgently with a senior paediatrician and referred to local safeguarding procedures, including children's social care. Discharge or routine follow-up would risk further harm. It is not necessary to wait for every detail to be confirmed before acting on safeguarding concerns. Clinicians should not confront parents aggressively or attempt to obtain confessions; the role is to assess, document and escalate appropriately.
clinical_context: UK clinicians have a duty to act when a child may be at risk of significant harm, sharing information when necessary for safeguarding.
simplified_explanation: A baby with an unexplained fracture and unusual bruising may be being harmed. The priority is to keep the child safe and involve safeguarding services.
guideline_anchor: NICE child maltreatment guidance and GMC safeguarding principles
exam_tip: If you suspect non-accidental injury, do not discharge; escalate through safeguarding pathways.
tested_concept: Immediate safeguarding management when non-accidental injury is suspected
learning_objective: Take appropriate action to protect a child when injuries and history raise concern for physical abuse.

rationale: This patient has acute severe asthma: oxygen saturation below 92%, respiratory rate above 25/min, heart rate above 110/min and PEF 33-50% of best or predicted. Immediate treatment includes oxygen to maintain adequate saturations, nebulised salbutamol, nebulised ipratropium in severe attacks, and systemic corticosteroids. Discharge is unsafe. Antibiotics are not routinely indicated unless there is evidence of bacterial infection. Starting or adjusting maintenance inhaled corticosteroid therapy is important later but not sufficient for the acute attack. Intravenous magnesium sulfate may be considered if there is poor response to initial therapy or life-threatening features, but it is not the sole initial treatment.
clinical_context: Acute severe asthma is a common UK emergency presentation requiring prompt bronchodilator therapy and early steroids.
simplified_explanation: Her asthma attack is severe. She needs oxygen, nebulised reliever treatment and steroids straight away.
guideline_anchor: British Thoracic Society/SIGN asthma guidance and NICE asthma guidance
exam_tip: In acute severe asthma, give oxygen, nebulised beta-agonist, add ipratropium, and give steroids early.
tested_concept: Immediate treatment of an acute severe asthma attack
learning_objective: Manage acute severe asthma with controlled oxygen, bronchodilator nebulisers and systemic corticosteroids.

rationale: Rosacea commonly presents in adults with central facial erythema, flushing triggered by alcohol, hot drinks or heat, telangiectasia, and papules or pustules. The absence of comedones helps distinguish it from acne vulgaris. Seborrhoeic dermatitis usually causes greasy scale in areas such as the nasolabial folds, scalp and eyebrows. Systemic lupus erythematosus may cause a photosensitive malar rash but typically spares the nasolabial folds and is not associated with pustules or flushing triggers. Perioral dermatitis mainly affects the area around the mouth and often spares the vermilion border.
clinical_context: Rosacea is commonly diagnosed clinically in primary care and dermatology clinics in the UK.
simplified_explanation: Rosacea causes redness and visible small blood vessels on the central face, often triggered by alcohol or hot drinks. It can cause spots but not blackheads or whiteheads.
guideline_anchor: NICE Clinical Knowledge Summary on rosacea
exam_tip: Adult facial flushing with telangiectasia and no comedones points to rosacea.
tested_concept: Recognition of papulopustular rosacea with flushing triggers and absence of comedones
learning_objective: Diagnose rosacea from central facial erythema, telangiectasia, flushing triggers and papules or pustules without comedones.

rationale: Gliclazide is a sulfonylurea and can cause prolonged or recurrent hypoglycaemia, especially in older adults. Recurrence after intravenous glucose strongly suggests ongoing insulin secretion driven by the sulfonylurea. The patient should be admitted for monitoring, the sulfonylurea stopped, glucose given as needed, and octreotide considered to suppress further insulin release. Discharge is unsafe because recurrent hypoglycaemia may be prolonged. Glucagon may have a temporary effect but is not definitive and does not remove the need for monitoring. Restarting gliclazide is inappropriate. Insulin would worsen hypoglycaemia.
clinical_context: Sulfonylurea-induced hypoglycaemia is an important cause of recurrent hypoglycaemia in older adults and often needs prolonged observation in hospital.
simplified_explanation: Gliclazide can keep pushing the pancreas to release insulin, so low blood sugar can come back even after glucose. Octreotide helps stop this repeated insulin release.
guideline_anchor: BNF and standard UK emergency diabetes practice
exam_tip: Recurrent hypoglycaemia in a patient on a sulfonylurea should make you think of octreotide and admission.
tested_concept: Management of recurrent sulfonylurea-induced hypoglycaemia
learning_objective: Recognise that sulfonylurea hypoglycaemia can recur and requires admission, monitoring, glucose support and consideration of octreotide.

rationale: This is typical biliary colic: episodic post-prandial right upper quadrant pain with normal inflammatory markers, liver tests and amylase. Abdominal ultrasound is the first-line test for gallstones. CT is less sensitive for uncomplicated gallstones and is not first line. ERCP is therapeutic and reserved for confirmed or strongly suspected common bile duct stones or cholangitis. HIDA scanning is mainly used when acute cholecystitis is suspected but ultrasound is inconclusive. MRCP is used when common bile duct stones are suspected, particularly with abnormal liver tests or duct dilatation.
clinical_context: In UK practice, uncomplicated biliary colic is usually investigated initially with liver blood tests and transabdominal ultrasound before referral for consideration of laparoscopic cholecystectomy.
simplified_explanation: Gallstones are best looked for first with an ultrasound scan. More invasive or advanced tests are used only if there are signs that a stone is stuck in the bile duct or complications have developed.
guideline_anchor: NICE clinical knowledge summaries and standard UK surgical practice
exam_tip: Biliary colic plus normal blood tests: choose abdominal ultrasound first.
tested_concept: First-line imaging for suspected uncomplicated gallstones causing biliary colic
learning_objective: Select abdominal ultrasound as the initial investigation for suspected gallstones when there are no features of cholangitis, pancreatitis or common bile duct obstruction.

rationale: The key additional feature beyond acute severe colitis is marked colonic dilatation on abdominal X-ray with systemic toxicity, which indicates toxic megacolon. Acute severe ulcerative colitis alone causes frequent bloody stools and raised inflammatory markers but does not require colonic dilatation. C difficile can precipitate toxic megacolon but is not the best unifying diagnosis from the information given. Ischaemic colitis is more typical in older patients or vascular risk and usually has segmental pain and bleeding. Mechanical obstruction would not usually cause bloody diarrhoea in a known UC flare and systemic inflammatory colitis picture.
clinical_context: Toxic megacolon is a surgical and medical emergency requiring close monitoring, resuscitation, intravenous steroids or antibiotics as appropriate, and early colorectal surgical involvement.
simplified_explanation: Severe colitis becomes toxic megacolon when the colon becomes dangerously swollen and the patient is systemically unwell.
guideline_anchor: NICE and British Society of Gastroenterology principles for acute severe colitis; standard UK surgical practice
exam_tip: Colitis plus fever/tachycardia plus colon diameter over 6 cm is toxic megacolon.
tested_concept: Recognising toxic megacolon from systemic toxicity and radiological colonic dilatation in colitis
learning_objective: Diagnose toxic megacolon when acute colitis is complicated by systemic toxicity and colonic dilatation greater than about 6 cm.

rationale: For advanced epithelial ovarian cancer, standard first-line adjuvant chemotherapy is a platinum agent, commonly carboplatin, combined with paclitaxel. Anastrozole and tamoxifen are endocrine therapies used in selected hormone-sensitive cancers and are not standard first-line adjuvant treatment for high-grade serous ovarian cancer. Cisplatin and bleomycin are more relevant to some germ cell tumour regimens. Methotrexate with folinic acid is used in gestational trophoblastic disease and some other settings, not typical epithelial ovarian cancer.
clinical_context: In UK oncology practice, women with advanced epithelial ovarian cancer are managed by a gynaecological oncology multidisciplinary team with surgery and platinum-based chemotherapy, with additional targeted or maintenance treatments considered according to tumour and patient factors.
simplified_explanation: The usual chemotherapy backbone for advanced epithelial ovarian cancer is carboplatin plus paclitaxel.
guideline_anchor: NICE ovarian cancer guidance and standard UK oncology practice
exam_tip: High-grade epithelial ovarian cancer: think debulking surgery plus carboplatin-paclitaxel.
tested_concept: Standard adjuvant chemotherapy for advanced epithelial ovarian cancer
learning_objective: Choose platinum-taxane chemotherapy as standard systemic treatment after surgery for advanced epithelial ovarian cancer.

rationale: A persistent dry cough starting after initiation of an ACE inhibitor is a classic adverse effect. The appropriate management is to stop ramipril and use another antihypertensive, commonly an angiotensin II receptor blocker if renin-angiotensin system blockade remains suitable. Inhaled steroids are not indicated without asthma or eosinophilic airway disease. CT chest is unnecessary without red flags or abnormal examination. Continuing ramipril is likely to perpetuate the adverse effect. Antibiotics are not indicated in the absence of infection.
clinical_context: ACE inhibitor cough is common in primary care and outpatient medicine. ARBs are generally much less likely to cause cough.
simplified_explanation: Ramipril can cause a dry cough. The usual fix is to stop it and use a similar blood pressure medicine that does not commonly cause cough.
guideline_anchor: BNF and NICE hypertension guidance principles
exam_tip: Dry cough after starting an ACE inhibitor: switch to an ARB.
tested_concept: Management of ACE inhibitor-induced cough
learning_objective: Recognise ACE inhibitor cough and manage it by stopping the ACE inhibitor and switching to an alternative such as an angiotensin II receptor blocker when appropriate.

rationale: Faltering growth with abdominal bloating, bulky pale stools and microcytic anaemia suggests malabsorption due to coeliac disease. The appropriate initial investigation is IgA tissue transglutaminase antibody with total IgA, as IgA deficiency can cause false-negative IgA-based tests. Faecal calprotectin is more useful for inflammatory bowel disease. IGF-1 may be used in suspected growth hormone deficiency but does not fit the gastrointestinal symptoms. Stool culture is for suspected infection. Sweat chloride tests cystic fibrosis, which can cause malabsorption, but the iron deficiency, bloating and classic coeliac symptoms make coeliac serology the best first investigation.
clinical_context: Children with faltering growth require careful growth assessment, dietary history and targeted investigation for common treatable causes such as coeliac disease.
simplified_explanation: This child is not absorbing food properly. Coeliac disease is a common cause and is screened for with a blood antibody test plus a check of total IgA.
guideline_anchor: NICE coeliac disease guidance and NICE faltering growth principles
exam_tip: Faltering growth plus bloating, pale stools and iron deficiency: test for coeliac disease.
tested_concept: Investigating coeliac disease as a cause of faltering growth and malabsorption
learning_objective: Select coeliac serology, including total IgA, in a child with faltering growth, malabsorptive stools and iron deficiency anaemia.

rationale: This is exertional heat stroke: core temperature above 40°C with central nervous system dysfunction after exertion in heat. Immediate rapid active cooling is the priority; cold-water immersion is highly effective if it can be done safely while monitoring ABCs. Dantrolene is used for malignant hyperthermia, not exertional heat stroke. CT head may be needed later if another cause is suspected, but cooling must not be delayed. Paracetamol treats fever due to hypothalamic set-point change and is ineffective in heat stroke. Waiting for blood results is unsafe.
clinical_context: Heat stroke is time-critical. In UK emergency care, resuscitation and rapid cooling are started immediately, with monitoring for complications such as rhabdomyolysis, acute kidney injury, coagulopathy and electrolyte disturbance.
simplified_explanation: This is dangerous overheating, not ordinary fever. The body must be cooled quickly while the airway, breathing and circulation are supported.
guideline_anchor: Resus Council UK principles and standard UK emergency medicine practice
exam_tip: Heat stroke equals hot, confused and very high core temperature: cool first, do not rely on paracetamol.
tested_concept: Immediate management of exertional heat stroke
learning_objective: Manage heat stroke with urgent active cooling and supportive resuscitation rather than antipyretics or delayed investigation.

rationale: Cervical ectropion occurs when columnar epithelium is visible on the ectocervix, producing a red, velvety appearance and contact bleeding. It is common in younger women and with combined hormonal contraception. Cervical intraepithelial neoplasia cannot be diagnosed by appearance alone and would be more concerning with abnormal screening or suspicious lesions. Chlamydial cervicitis can cause contact bleeding but usually has mucopurulent discharge or cervicitis; STI testing may still be appropriate. An endometrial polyp causes intermenstrual bleeding and is not seen as a red area around the os. Lichen sclerosus affects the vulva, not the cervix.
clinical_context: Post-coital bleeding should be assessed with pregnancy testing, STI consideration and speculum examination. Benign ectropion can be managed conservatively if symptoms are mild and other causes are excluded.
simplified_explanation: Cervical ectropion is a harmless area of delicate glandular cells on the outside of the cervix. These cells can look red and bleed when touched.
guideline_anchor: NICE clinical knowledge summaries and standard UK gynaecology practice
exam_tip: Red velvety tissue around the cervical os in a young woman on the pill suggests ectropion.
tested_concept: Recognition of cervical ectropion in a young woman with contact bleeding and a red ectocervical appearance
learning_objective: Diagnose cervical ectropion from post-coital bleeding with a benign red, velvety area around the external os, especially in association with oestrogen exposure.

rationale: Typhoid fever is suggested by prolonged fever after travel to Pakistan, relative bradycardia, abdominal symptoms and rose spots, confirmed by blood culture. In a hospitalised patient unable to take oral treatment, intravenous ceftriaxone is an appropriate empirical choice while sensitivities are awaited. Ciprofloxacin should not be used empirically for South Asia-acquired typhoid because resistance and reduced susceptibility are common; it may be used only if susceptibility is confirmed. Oral azithromycin can be used in some uncomplicated cases but is less suitable here because he cannot maintain oral intake. Co-amoxiclav and doxycycline are not standard empirical treatments for typhoid.
clinical_context: Imported enteric fever in the UK should involve microbiology or infectious diseases advice, public health notification and antibiotic selection guided by travel region and susceptibility results.
simplified_explanation: Typhoid from South Asia is often resistant to older oral options such as ciprofloxacin. A sick patient who cannot take tablets is usually treated initially with IV ceftriaxone.
guideline_anchor: BNF, UKHSA principles and standard UK infectious diseases practice
exam_tip: Typhoid after travel to South Asia: avoid empirical ciprofloxacin unless sensitivities support it.
tested_concept: Empirical antibiotic choice for hospitalised enteric fever acquired in South Asia
learning_objective: Choose intravenous ceftriaxone for a systemically unwell or unable-to-take-oral patient with suspected or confirmed typhoid acquired in an area with significant fluoroquinolone resistance.

rationale: Confusion, ataxia and nystagmus in a malnourished patient with alcohol dependence is Wernicke’s encephalopathy until proven otherwise. Immediate high-dose parenteral thiamine is required to prevent irreversible Korsakoff syndrome or death. Oral thiamine is inadequate for acute suspected Wernicke’s. MRI can support the diagnosis but must not delay treatment. Chlordiazepoxide may be needed for alcohol withdrawal but does not treat Wernicke’s and should not be the first action here. Outpatient follow-up is unsafe.
clinical_context: In UK emergency care, suspected Wernicke’s encephalopathy is treated immediately with intravenous high-potency thiamine preparations and admission for monitoring and nutritional support.
simplified_explanation: This patient’s brain may be short of thiamine. It is an emergency, and thiamine must be given into a vein straight away.
guideline_anchor: BNF and NICE alcohol-use disorders guidance principles
exam_tip: Alcohol dependence plus confusion, ataxia or eye signs: give parenteral thiamine now.
tested_concept: Emergency treatment of suspected Wernicke’s encephalopathy
learning_objective: Treat suspected Wernicke’s encephalopathy urgently with parenteral thiamine without waiting for imaging or laboratory confirmation.

rationale: Fever with cough, coryza, conjunctivitis, Koplik spots and a cephalocaudal maculopapular rash in an unimmunised child is highly suggestive of measles. Measles is notifiable; the child should be isolated and the local health protection team notified. Aciclovir is for varicella or herpes infections in selected cases, not measles. Amoxicillin is not indicated for an uncomplicated viral exanthem. Infection control remains important after rash onset because measles is highly contagious. The child should not attend school during the infectious period.
clinical_context: Suspected measles in UK primary care requires prompt infection control measures, notification and advice about exclusion, vaccination status of contacts and protection of vulnerable contacts.
simplified_explanation: This looks like measles. Because measles spreads easily and can be serious, the child should be kept away from others and public health teams must be informed.
guideline_anchor: UKHSA measles guidance and notifiable disease regulations
exam_tip: Koplik spots plus cough, coryza, conjunctivitis and rash: think measles and notify.
tested_concept: Management of suspected measles with infection control and public health notification
learning_objective: Recognise measles as a viral exanthem and take appropriate public health action, including isolation and notification.

rationale: The combination of heavy alcohol intake, recent jaundice, fever, tender hepatomegaly, neutrophilia and AST greater than ALT with transaminases usually below the very high levels seen in viral or ischaemic hepatitis is most consistent with acute alcoholic hepatitis. Ascending cholangitis would usually have biliary obstruction or duct dilatation and more marked cholestatic features. Acute viral hepatitis often causes much higher ALT and AST, commonly with ALT predominance. Autoimmune hepatitis is possible in jaundice but is less likely with this alcohol history and typical AST:ALT pattern. Gilbert syndrome causes isolated mild unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia without systemic illness or abnormal INR.
clinical_context: In UK acute medical and gastroenterology practice, alcoholic hepatitis is a clinical diagnosis supported by liver tests and imaging to exclude biliary obstruction or other causes.
simplified_explanation: Alcoholic hepatitis often causes jaundice, fever and a sore enlarged liver. The AST is usually higher than the ALT, but neither is usually in the thousands.
guideline_anchor: NICE and standard UK hepatology practice
exam_tip: In alcoholic hepatitis, think jaundice plus systemic inflammation plus AST:ALT ratio greater than 2 in a heavy drinker.
tested_concept: Recognition of acute alcoholic hepatitis from jaundice, systemic inflammation and an AST-predominant transaminitis in a heavy alcohol user
learning_objective: Diagnose alcoholic hepatitis in a patient with heavy alcohol use, jaundice, tender hepatomegaly and AST greater than ALT with only moderate transaminase elevation.

rationale: A core biopsy of an accessible liver metastasis can provide histological confirmation and confirms metastatic disease, which is important before palliative chemotherapy. CA19-9 may support monitoring but is not diagnostic and can be elevated in benign biliary disease. ERCP brush cytology is mainly used when sampling a biliary stricture or relieving obstruction, which is not the issue in a pancreatic tail lesion. PET-CT may provide staging information in selected cases but does not provide tissue diagnosis. Repeating CT would delay diagnosis without adding histology.
clinical_context: UK pancreatic cancer pathways use pancreatic protocol CT for staging, with tissue confirmation required before non-surgical oncological treatment where feasible.
simplified_explanation: If pancreatic cancer has already spread and chemotherapy is planned, doctors usually need a tissue sample. A liver deposit is often the easiest and safest place to biopsy.
guideline_anchor: NICE pancreatic cancer guidance and standard UK hepatopancreatobiliary MDT practice
exam_tip: Tumour markers do not replace histology when chemotherapy is being planned for metastatic pancreatic cancer.
tested_concept: Obtaining histological confirmation in metastatic suspected pancreatic cancer before systemic treatment
learning_objective: Select biopsy of an accessible metastatic lesion as an appropriate way to confirm suspected metastatic pancreatic cancer before chemotherapy.

rationale: Tamsulosin is an alpha-blocker used as medical expulsive therapy and may aid passage of distal ureteric stones in adults. Bendroflumethiazide may reduce recurrence in selected patients with hypercalciuria but does not help acute passage. Ciprofloxacin is not indicated without evidence of infection. Potassium citrate can be used for selected uric acid stones or recurrence prevention, not acute distal ureteric stone passage. Tranexamic acid is not used for ureteric colic and could worsen clot obstruction if haematuria were significant.
clinical_context: In UK emergency and urology practice, stable patients with small distal ureteric stones may be managed conservatively with analgesia, safety-netting and consideration of an alpha-blocker.
simplified_explanation: Tamsulosin relaxes smooth muscle in the ureter and can help a lower ureter stone pass.
guideline_anchor: NICE renal and ureteric stones guidance; BNF prescribing principles
exam_tip: For a stable adult with a distal ureteric stone less than 10 mm, consider an alpha-blocker.
tested_concept: Use of alpha-blockers as medical expulsive therapy for distal ureteric stones
learning_objective: Prescribe an alpha-blocker for a stable adult with a distal ureteric stone suitable for conservative management.

rationale: Medical information must not be disclosed to an employer without the patient's explicit consent, unless there is an overriding public interest or legal requirement. Essential thrombocythaemia can increase thrombotic risk but does not by itself justify breaching confidentiality to an employer. Confirming the diagnosis, disclosing a platelet count or sending clinic letters would all reveal confidential information. The appropriate response is to decline disclosure and seek the patient's consent if occupational information is required.
clinical_context: Clinicians in UK haematology clinics commonly receive third-party requests, but confidentiality remains central unless a clear legal or public interest exception applies.
simplified_explanation: An employer cannot be given a patient's diagnosis or blood results unless the patient agrees, except in rare situations where others are at serious risk.
guideline_anchor: GMC confidentiality guidance
exam_tip: For employer requests, the default is no disclosure without the patient's consent.
tested_concept: Confidentiality in a patient with a myeloproliferative neoplasm when an employer requests medical information
learning_objective: Apply GMC confidentiality principles to requests from third parties about a patient's haematological diagnosis.

rationale: Contrast-enhanced CT is the appropriate investigation after the initial early phase when there is clinical deterioration or failure to improve, as it can assess pancreatic necrosis and collections. Abdominal X-ray is not useful for assessing pancreatic complications. ERCP is indicated for selected patients with cholangitis or persistent biliary obstruction, not simply to assess necrosis. Repeat amylase does not correlate with severity or complications. Ultrasound may identify gallstones or biliary dilatation but is poor for assessing pancreatic necrosis.
clinical_context: In UK acute pancreatitis pathways, CT is not routinely needed at presentation if the diagnosis is clear, but is used when severe disease or complications are suspected after 48-72 hours.
simplified_explanation: If pancreatitis is not improving after a few days, a contrast CT can show whether part of the pancreas has died or whether collections have formed.
guideline_anchor: NICE pancreatitis guidance and standard UK surgical/gastroenterology practice
exam_tip: Do not use serial amylase to monitor pancreatitis severity; use contrast CT when complications are suspected.
tested_concept: Use of contrast-enhanced CT after the early phase of severe or non-improving acute pancreatitis to assess complications
learning_objective: Choose contrast-enhanced CT when acute pancreatitis fails to improve or severe complications such as necrosis are suspected.

rationale: A full-thickness rectal prolapse typically appears as a circumferential protrusion with concentric mucosal folds, often after straining and reducible initially. Prolapsing internal haemorrhoids tend to form separate radial columns rather than a circumferential ring with concentric folds. Anal carcinoma is usually an irregular mass, ulcer or indurated lesion rather than a reducible circumferential prolapse. A perianal haematoma is an acute painful bluish perianal lump. A rectocele is a bulge of the anterior rectal wall into the vagina and would not appear as a circumferential anal protrusion.
clinical_context: Rectal prolapse is commonly assessed in UK colorectal surgery and primary care, particularly in older women and patients with pelvic floor weakness.
simplified_explanation: A full rectal prolapse comes out as a complete ring of rectum, giving circular folds all the way round.
guideline_anchor: standard UK colorectal practice
exam_tip: Concentric circular folds point to full-thickness rectal prolapse; radial columns suggest haemorrhoids.
tested_concept: Recognition of full-thickness rectal prolapse by circumferential protrusion with concentric folds
learning_objective: Differentiate full-thickness rectal prolapse from prolapsing haemorrhoids using examination findings.

rationale: A varicocele is dilatation of the pampiniform plexus and classically feels like a 'bag of worms', is usually left-sided, worsens on standing and reduces when supine. A hydrocoele is a fluid swelling around the testis that transilluminates and is not described as a bag of worms. An epididymal cyst or spermatocele is usually a discrete cystic swelling separate from the testis and does not characteristically reduce on lying down. An indirect inguinal hernia may have a cough impulse and extend from the groin, rather than being a venous-feeling swelling above the testis.
clinical_context: Benign scrotal swellings are common in UK primary care and urology; examination position and transillumination help differentiate them.
simplified_explanation: A varicocele is like varicose veins around the testicle, so it feels like a soft bag of worms and often disappears when lying flat.
guideline_anchor: standard UK urology practice
exam_tip: Bag of worms plus left-sided swelling worse on standing equals varicocele.
tested_concept: Clinical diagnosis of varicocele from a left-sided 'bag of worms' swelling that reduces when supine
learning_objective: Recognise the typical examination features of a varicocele and distinguish it from other benign scrotal swellings.

rationale: Saddle numbness, urinary difficulty, reduced anal tone and bilateral neurological signs are red flags for cauda equina syndrome and require immediate emergency assessment and urgent MRI/spinal surgical input. Attributing these symptoms to fibromyalgia would be unsafe. Routine MRI, analgesia review or routine pain clinic referral would delay time-critical management. Oral prednisolone is not appropriate for this red-flag presentation.
clinical_context: In UK primary care and emergency practice, cauda equina symptoms require same-day emergency referral regardless of a pre-existing chronic pain diagnosis.
simplified_explanation: Fibromyalgia causes chronic widespread pain, but it does not cause numbness in the saddle area or bladder problems. These signs can mean pressure on the nerves at the bottom of the spine.
guideline_anchor: NICE low back pain/sciatica guidance and standard UK emergency spinal pathway principles
exam_tip: Do not let a fibromyalgia label distract from new objective neurological red flags.
tested_concept: Avoiding diagnostic overshadowing in fibromyalgia when red flags suggest cauda equina syndrome
learning_objective: Escalate urgently when a patient with chronic widespread pain develops saddle sensory disturbance, urinary symptoms and neurological signs.

rationale: ARDS severity is classified using oxygenation impairment, particularly the PaO2/FiO2 ratio, in a patient with acute bilateral opacities not fully explained by cardiac failure or fluid overload. An arterial blood gas provides the PaO2 needed for this calculation. Bronchoscopy may help identify infection but does not classify ARDS severity. CT pulmonary angiography investigates pulmonary embolism. D-dimer is non-specific in ICU patients. BNP may support assessment of cardiac failure but is not the key measure of ARDS severity.
clinical_context: In UK intensive care, ARDS is assessed using clinical context, imaging and oxygenation parameters, with ABG values guiding severity classification and ventilatory management.
simplified_explanation: ARDS severity depends on how poorly oxygen is passing from the lungs into the blood. An arterial blood gas gives the oxygen level needed to calculate this.
guideline_anchor: Berlin definition of ARDS and standard UK intensive care practice
exam_tip: For ARDS severity, think PaO2/FiO2 ratio, not oxygen saturations alone.
tested_concept: Use of PaO2/FiO2 ratio to assess ARDS severity in the context of acute bilateral infiltrates not explained by cardiac failure
learning_objective: Select arterial blood gas analysis for calculating the PaO2/FiO2 ratio when assessing ARDS severity.

rationale: Loss of both temporal visual fields suggests bitemporal hemianopia from optic chiasm compression, commonly due to a pituitary macroadenoma. Headache and reduced libido further support pituitary disease. Urgent MRI of the pituitary region and referral to endocrinology/neurosurgery or ophthalmology is appropriate. Latanoprost is used for glaucoma, which typically causes different visual field patterns. Optic neuritis usually causes painful monocular visual loss. Lubricants, reassurance or routine review would be inappropriate and risk delayed diagnosis.
clinical_context: In UK eye care and primary care, suspected chiasmal visual field defects require urgent neuroimaging and specialist assessment.
simplified_explanation: Losing the outer half of vision in both eyes points to pressure where the optic nerves cross, often from a pituitary tumour.
guideline_anchor: NICE suspected neurological conditions principles and standard UK ophthalmology/endocrinology practice
exam_tip: Bitemporal hemianopia localises to the optic chiasm until proven otherwise.
tested_concept: Management of bitemporal visual field loss suggesting optic chiasm compression by a pituitary mass
learning_objective: Recognise bitemporal hemianopia as a chiasmal lesion requiring urgent pituitary imaging and specialist referral.

rationale: This patient has scleroderma renal crisis: abrupt severe hypertension, acute kidney injury and microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia in diffuse systemic sclerosis, with corticosteroid exposure as a risk factor. ACE inhibitors, commonly captopril because it is short acting and titratable, are the key treatment and should be started urgently. Labetalol may lower blood pressure but does not target the renin-angiotensin mechanism driving the crisis. Nifedipine is used for Raynaud's phenomenon rather than renal crisis. Further prednisolone may worsen risk. Cyclophosphamide is used for some severe systemic sclerosis complications such as interstitial lung disease, not acute renal crisis.
clinical_context: In UK practice, suspected scleroderma renal crisis requires urgent senior, renal and rheumatology involvement, but ACE inhibitor treatment should not be delayed.
simplified_explanation: Systemic sclerosis can suddenly cause very high blood pressure and kidney failure. The best immediate drug is an ACE inhibitor such as captopril.
guideline_anchor: standard UK rheumatology practice; BNF prescribing principles for ACE inhibitors
exam_tip: In systemic sclerosis, sudden hypertension plus renal failure equals scleroderma renal crisis: start an ACE inhibitor.
tested_concept: Treatment of scleroderma renal crisis with an ACE inhibitor
learning_objective: Recognise scleroderma renal crisis and prescribe urgent ACE inhibitor therapy, even when renal function is impaired.

rationale: Schizotypal personality disorder is characterised by longstanding social and interpersonal difficulties with eccentric behaviour, odd speech, magical thinking or ideas of reference, without persistent psychosis. Paranoid schizophrenia would involve sustained delusions, hallucinations or thought disorder. Schizoid personality disorder involves detachment and limited emotional expression but not marked odd beliefs or ideas of reference. Avoidant personality disorder is driven by fear of criticism and rejection. Autism spectrum disorder may cause social communication difficulties and restricted interests, but the stem emphasises odd beliefs and ideas of reference emerging as a personality pattern.
clinical_context: Personality disorder diagnoses should be made carefully, usually after longitudinal assessment and consideration of neurodevelopmental, mood and psychotic disorders.
simplified_explanation: This is a lifelong pattern of being socially detached and eccentric, with unusual beliefs but not full psychosis.
guideline_anchor: NICE principles for assessment of personality disorders and standard UK psychiatric practice
exam_tip: Odd beliefs and ideas of reference without sustained psychosis point towards schizotypal personality disorder.
tested_concept: Recognition of schizotypal personality disorder
learning_objective: Differentiate schizotypal personality disorder from schizophrenia, schizoid personality disorder, avoidant personality disorder and autism spectrum disorder.

rationale: Laryngospasm is a reflex closure of the vocal cords causing acute upper airway obstruction, classically after extubation and triggered by secretions or blood. It causes inspiratory effort, tracheal tug, poor or absent air movement and desaturation. Bronchospasm usually causes wheeze and prolonged expiration with some ventilation possible. Aspiration pneumonitis may cause hypoxia but not sudden complete upper airway obstruction. Anaphylaxis would usually involve hypotension, rash or bronchospasm. Tension pneumothorax would cause unilateral chest signs and haemodynamic compromise.
clinical_context: Post-extubation airway obstruction is a perioperative emergency requiring immediate anaesthetic management, including airway manoeuvres, positive pressure and, if needed, suxamethonium.
simplified_explanation: After the breathing tube is removed, blood or secretions can make the vocal cords clamp shut, blocking airflow.
guideline_anchor: Resuscitation Council UK and standard UK anaesthetic airway management principles
exam_tip: After extubation, sudden obstructed inspiration with minimal air entry suggests laryngospasm.
tested_concept: Recognition of post-extubation laryngospasm
learning_objective: Identify laryngospasm as a cause of acute upper airway obstruction after extubation, particularly with airway stimulation or blood in the pharynx.

rationale: Confusion with asterixis in a patient with cirrhosis is hepatic encephalopathy, with constipation as a common precipitant. Lactulose is first-line because it reduces intestinal ammonia absorption and treats constipation. Haloperidol may be used cautiously for severe agitation but does not treat the cause and can worsen sedation. Terlipressin is used in variceal bleeding or hepatorenal syndrome. Spironolactone is used for ascites. Propranolol is used for prevention of variceal bleeding and may be inappropriate in acute decompensation.
clinical_context: UK management of hepatic encephalopathy includes identifying and treating precipitants, giving lactulose and considering rifaximin for recurrent episodes or inadequate response.
simplified_explanation: Liver failure can allow toxins from the bowel to affect the brain. Lactulose helps clear these toxins and relieves constipation.
guideline_anchor: NICE cirrhosis guidance and BNF prescribing principles
exam_tip: Cirrhosis plus confusion and flapping tremor: treat hepatic encephalopathy with lactulose and look for triggers.
tested_concept: Initial drug treatment of hepatic encephalopathy
learning_objective: Prescribe lactulose as first-line treatment for hepatic encephalopathy in a patient with cirrhosis.

rationale: After appropriate assessment has excluded an acute emergency, the best approach is to validate that the symptoms are real, explain the reassuring findings, provide safety-net advice and support continuity through the GP. Admission for repeated broad investigation is not indicated without new red flags. Discharging without explanation is dismissive and may increase anxiety and reattendance. Regular diazepam risks dependence and does not address the problem. Neurology referral is not indicated for transient tingling associated with chest tightness and a normal assessment unless focal neurological signs are present.
clinical_context: Emergency clinicians should avoid diagnostic overshadowing but also avoid iatrogenic harm from repeated low-yield tests once acute pathology has been reasonably excluded.
simplified_explanation: When tests are reassuring, the patient still needs to be taken seriously, given a clear explanation and offered follow-up rather than repeated unnecessary scans.
guideline_anchor: standard UK clinical practice and NICE principles for patient-centred assessment
exam_tip: For medically unexplained symptoms, validate the symptoms; do not say 'nothing is wrong'.
tested_concept: Management of medically unexplained symptoms after appropriate acute assessment
learning_objective: Manage recurrent medically unexplained symptoms with validation, clear explanation, safety-netting and planned follow-up rather than repeated unnecessary investigations.

rationale: Neuroleptic malignant syndrome follows dopamine antagonist use or dose increase and causes fever, altered mental state, autonomic instability, lead-pipe rigidity and markedly raised CK. Serotonin syndrome is more associated with serotonergic drugs, hyperreflexia, clonus and gastrointestinal symptoms. Malignant hyperthermia occurs in relation to anaesthetic agents such as suxamethonium or volatile anaesthetics. Acute dystonia causes focal muscle spasms without severe hyperthermia and CK elevation. Anticholinergic toxicity causes dry skin, mydriasis, urinary retention and delirium rather than severe rigidity.
clinical_context: NMS is a medical emergency requiring stopping the antipsychotic, supportive care, fluid resuscitation and urgent senior medical input.
simplified_explanation: A recent increase in antipsychotic medication followed by fever, confusion, stiff muscles and very high CK is neuroleptic malignant syndrome.
guideline_anchor: standard UK psychiatric and acute medical practice; BNF adverse drug reaction principles
exam_tip: NMS has lead-pipe rigidity and hyporeflexia; serotonin syndrome has clonus and hyperreflexia.
tested_concept: Distinguishing neuroleptic malignant syndrome from serotonin syndrome and other hyperthermic states
learning_objective: Recognise neuroleptic malignant syndrome from recent dopamine antagonist exposure, hyperthermia, autonomic instability, altered mental state, rigidity and raised creatine kinase.

rationale: Ankylosing spondylitis is associated with acute anterior uveitis, which presents with painful red eye, photophobia and blurred vision. It requires same-day ophthalmology assessment to prevent complications. Chloramphenicol is for bacterial conjunctivitis, which usually has discharge and gritty discomfort rather than photophobia and visual blurring. Lubricants and reassurance are unsafe. Topical steroids may be needed but should be initiated under ophthalmology guidance because alternative diagnoses such as herpetic keratitis must be excluded.
clinical_context: In UK primary and emergency care, a painful red eye with photophobia or reduced vision is an urgent ophthalmology presentation.
simplified_explanation: Ankylosing spondylitis can inflame the front of the eye. Pain, light sensitivity and blurred vision need same-day eye specialist review.
guideline_anchor: NICE CKS red eye principles and standard UK ophthalmology practice
exam_tip: Painful photophobic red eye in ankylosing spondylitis is anterior uveitis until proven otherwise.
tested_concept: Urgent escalation for suspected acute anterior uveitis in ankylosing spondylitis
learning_objective: Recognise painful photophobic red eye in seronegative spondyloarthropathy as possible anterior uveitis requiring same-day specialist assessment.

rationale: SJS/TEN is primarily a clinical diagnosis, but urgent skin biopsy can confirm full-thickness epidermal necrosis and help exclude mimics such as autoimmune blistering disease or staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome. Bacterial swabs may detect secondary infection but do not confirm SJS/TEN. ANA is not diagnostic. Patch testing is not an acute diagnostic test and is not routinely useful during the acute illness. Tryptase may support anaphylaxis or mast-cell activation, not SJS/TEN.
clinical_context: Suspected SJS/TEN requires immediate withdrawal of the culprit drug, urgent dermatology involvement and transfer to an appropriate specialist setting; biopsy should not delay emergency care.
simplified_explanation: A small skin sample can show the characteristic severe death of the top skin layer seen in SJS/TEN.
guideline_anchor: British Association of Dermatologists principles and standard UK dermatology practice
exam_tip: SJS/TEN is clinical, but biopsy is the confirmatory test when the diagnosis is uncertain.
tested_concept: Diagnostic confirmation of SJS/TEN with skin biopsy
learning_objective: Select urgent skin biopsy as the investigation to support diagnosis of SJS/TEN and distinguish it from other blistering disorders.

rationale: Syncope without warning, occurring while sitting and preceded by palpitations suggests an arrhythmic cause. Because episodes are infrequent, a 24-hour Holter monitor is unlikely to capture an event. An implantable loop recorder provides long-term rhythm monitoring and is appropriate. EEG is not indicated when the history favours syncope rather than epilepsy. Tilt-table testing is more useful for suspected reflex syncope when arrhythmia is less likely. Carotid Doppler ultrasound does not investigate syncope unless there are focal neurological features suggesting vascular disease.
clinical_context: UK assessment of transient loss of consciousness includes ECG for all patients and targeted ambulatory ECG monitoring when arrhythmia is suspected.
simplified_explanation: If fainting episodes are months apart, short heart monitors often miss them. A loop recorder can monitor the rhythm for much longer.
guideline_anchor: NICE guidance on transient loss of consciousness in adults and young people
exam_tip: Choose ambulatory ECG duration based on symptom frequency; very infrequent suspected arrhythmias need long-term monitoring.
tested_concept: Investigation of infrequent suspected arrhythmic syncope
learning_objective: Choose prolonged ECG monitoring, such as an implantable loop recorder, for infrequent episodes of suspected arrhythmic syncope.

rationale: Carbon monoxide poisoning causes non-specific symptoms such as headache, dizziness and nausea. Clustering among household members, worsening at home and improvement away from home strongly suggest an environmental exposure. Pulse oximetry may be falsely normal because it cannot reliably distinguish oxyhaemoglobin from carboxyhaemoglobin. A carboxyhaemoglobin level of 19% in a non-smoker supports the diagnosis. Viral gastroenteritis would not typically improve away from home and recur on return. Cyanide poisoning is usually associated with smoke inhalation or industrial exposure and severe lactic acidosis. Meningitis would usually cause fever, neck stiffness or altered consciousness. Salicylate poisoning causes tinnitus, hyperventilation and acid-base disturbance.
clinical_context: Suspected carbon monoxide poisoning requires high-flow oxygen, assessment of severity and advice to avoid returning to the exposure until the source is made safe.
simplified_explanation: Several people becoming unwell at home, improving away and having a raised carboxyhaemoglobin level is carbon monoxide poisoning. A normal oxygen saturation does not exclude it.
guideline_anchor: UKHSA and standard UK emergency medicine practice
exam_tip: Normal pulse oximetry does not rule out carbon monoxide poisoning.
tested_concept: Recognition of carbon monoxide poisoning despite normal pulse oximetry
learning_objective: Diagnose carbon monoxide poisoning from household clustering, symptoms that improve away from the exposure source and raised carboxyhaemoglobin.

rationale: This patient has established convulsive status epilepticus and has not responded to two doses of intravenous lorazepam. The next step is an intravenous longer-acting antiseizure medicine such as levetiracetam, alongside ongoing ABC support and senior escalation. A third benzodiazepine dose increases the risk of respiratory depression and is not the usual next step after two adequate doses. CT head may be needed later to identify a cause but must not delay seizure control. Oral carbamazepine is not appropriate in ongoing convulsive status epilepticus. Observation alone is unsafe.
clinical_context: In UK emergency departments, status epilepticus is managed using a stepwise protocol with early airway support, glucose correction, benzodiazepines, second-line intravenous antiseizure medication and escalation to anaesthesia or critical care if refractory.
simplified_explanation: If a seizure continues after two doses of lorazepam, move to a longer-acting intravenous anti-seizure drug rather than repeating sedatives or waiting.
guideline_anchor: NICE and Resus Council UK principles for convulsive status epilepticus management
exam_tip: After two adequate benzodiazepine doses, think second-line IV antiseizure therapy and senior escalation.
tested_concept: Second-line antiseizure treatment for established convulsive status epilepticus after benzodiazepines
learning_objective: Select an appropriate second-line intravenous antiseizure medicine when convulsive status epilepticus persists despite initial benzodiazepine treatment.

rationale: Posterior blepharitis is caused by meibomian gland dysfunction and presents with gritty, burning eyes, oily tear film, telangiectasia at the posterior lid margin and thick gland secretions. Anterior staphylococcal blepharitis more typically causes crusting and collarettes around the eyelashes. A chalazion is a discrete, usually painless tarsal plate lump. Entropion is inward turning of the eyelid causing lashes to rub on the eye. Xanthelasma causes yellow plaques around the eyelids rather than inflamed gland openings.
clinical_context: Meibomian gland dysfunction is common in primary care and optometry presentations and is usually managed with lid hygiene, warm compresses and treatment of associated dry eye or rosacea when present.
simplified_explanation: Blocked oily glands along the eyelid margin can cause chronic irritation and recurrent lid lumps. This is posterior blepharitis.
guideline_anchor: standard UK clinical practice
exam_tip: Meibomian gland dysfunction points to posterior blepharitis; lash crusting points more towards anterior blepharitis.
tested_concept: Recognition of posterior blepharitis due to meibomian gland dysfunction
learning_objective: Differentiate posterior blepharitis from other benign eyelid disorders using lid margin and meibomian gland findings.

rationale: Cycloplegic drops can blur vision and affect accommodation, making driving unsafe. The doctor should clearly advise the patient not to drive until vision has recovered and help arrange safe transport. Covering one eye is not a safe workaround because it reduces depth perception and may not meet driving standards. Immediate DVLA notification is not the first step for a temporary, treatment-related impairment; disclosure without consent is considered only if a patient continues to drive despite clear advice and poses a serious risk. Physically taking keys is usually not appropriate except in exceptional immediate danger. Documentation alone is insufficient without clear safety advice.
clinical_context: Patients attending UK eye casualty may receive dilating or cycloplegic drops. Clinicians should warn about temporary visual impairment and driving safety.
simplified_explanation: If eye drops make vision blurry, the patient should not drive until vision returns to normal. The clinician should explain this and help them get home safely.
guideline_anchor: GMC confidentiality and public safety principles; DVLA visual standards principles
exam_tip: For driving risk, advise the patient first; consider breaching confidentiality only if they ignore advice and create serious risk to others.
tested_concept: Professional duty to advise a patient not to drive when treatment temporarily impairs vision
learning_objective: Apply GMC and road safety principles when eye disease or ophthalmic treatment may make driving unsafe.

rationale: Gambling machines and online slot games use unpredictable rewards delivered after an uncertain number of responses, which is a variable-ratio reinforcement schedule. This produces high and persistent response rates and is resistant to extinction. Fixed-interval reinforcement gives rewards after a set time interval. Negative reinforcement involves removing an unpleasant stimulus. Classical conditioning is learning by association between stimuli. Vicarious learning involves learning by observing others.
clinical_context: Understanding reinforcement schedules helps explain why gambling behaviours can persist despite harm and why behavioural interventions target triggers, urges and reward patterns.
simplified_explanation: Unpredictable wins are especially powerful because the person keeps trying, not knowing which attempt might pay out.
guideline_anchor: standard behavioural science principles used in UK mental health practice
exam_tip: Unpredictable reward after a variable number of responses equals variable-ratio reinforcement.
tested_concept: Variable-ratio reinforcement in gambling behaviour
learning_objective: Explain how unpredictable rewards maintain gambling behaviour through operant conditioning.

rationale: An unexplained unilateral pleural effusion should be investigated with image-guided diagnostic pleural aspiration, sending fluid for biochemistry, cytology and microbiology as appropriate. Bronchoscopy may be indicated later if an endobronchial lesion is suspected but is not the initial test to characterise the effusion. CT pulmonary angiography and D-dimer are used when pulmonary embolism is suspected. Peak flow does not investigate pleural fluid.
clinical_context: In UK respiratory practice, thoracic ultrasound is used to confirm a safe site for pleural aspiration and reduce complications.
simplified_explanation: When one side has unexplained fluid around the lung, take a guided sample of the fluid to find out whether it is due to cancer, infection or another cause.
guideline_anchor: British Thoracic Society pleural disease guidance and standard UK clinical practice
exam_tip: Unilateral unexplained effusion usually needs diagnostic aspiration unless there is a clear transudative cause such as obvious heart failure.
tested_concept: Initial investigation of an undiagnosed unilateral pleural effusion
learning_objective: Choose diagnostic pleural aspiration for an unexplained unilateral pleural effusion in a stable patient.

rationale: Imagine 10,000 healthcare workers. If 90% are immune, 9,000 are truly immune and 1,000 are not. With 95% sensitivity, 8,550 immune workers test positive. With 90% specificity, 10% of the 1,000 non-immune workers test falsely positive, giving 100 false positives. Positive predictive value is true positives divided by all positive tests: 8,550 divided by 8,650, which is about 98.8%, approximately 99%.
clinical_context: Varicella immunity testing is relevant in healthcare settings because susceptible staff exposed to varicella may require occupational health advice and post-exposure management.
simplified_explanation: Most people in this group are already immune, so a positive test is very likely to be a true positive.
guideline_anchor: standard epidemiological principles; UKHSA varicella occupational health principles
exam_tip: For predictive values, build a 2 by 2 table using an easy denominator such as 10,000.
tested_concept: Calculation of positive predictive value from prevalence, sensitivity and specificity
learning_objective: Calculate positive predictive value using a clinically relevant varicella immunity testing scenario.

rationale: Delusional perception occurs when a real, correctly perceived event is given a new, abnormal and delusional meaning. Here, the passer-by tying a shoelace is perceived normally but interpreted as proof of MI5 surveillance. An auditory hallucination is a perception of sound without an external stimulus. Delusional mood is a vague sense that something significant or ominous is happening before a delusion crystallises. Obsessional rumination is intrusive, repetitive thought recognised as originating from the person's own mind and usually resisted. An overvalued idea is an understandable but dominant belief, not held with delusional intensity.
clinical_context: Psychopathology terms are used in UK mental state examination to describe the form of abnormal experiences, not just their content.
simplified_explanation: The person really saw the shoelace being tied, but attached a false, fixed and highly personal meaning to it.
guideline_anchor: standard UK psychiatric psychopathology teaching
exam_tip: Normal perception plus delusional meaning equals delusional perception.
tested_concept: Identification of delusional perception as a primary delusional phenomenon
learning_objective: Distinguish delusional perception from hallucination, obsession, overvalued idea and delusional mood.

rationale: This is major antepartum haemorrhage in a woman with known placenta praevia, maternal shock and fetal bradycardia. The correct management is immediate senior obstetric, anaesthetic and neonatal involvement, activation of the major haemorrhage protocol, maternal resuscitation with blood products as required and emergency caesarean birth. Digital vaginal examination is contraindicated in placenta praevia because it may worsen bleeding. Outpatient management and waiting for further imaging are unsafe. Induction with vaginal prostaglandin is inappropriate with major placenta praevia, transverse lie and fetal compromise.
clinical_context: In UK maternity units, major antepartum haemorrhage is managed as an obstetric emergency with multidisciplinary response and maternal stabilisation alongside planning urgent birth when indicated.
simplified_explanation: Heavy bleeding from placenta praevia with shock and a slow fetal heart rate is an emergency: resuscitate the mother and deliver by emergency caesarean.
guideline_anchor: RCOG and NICE principles for antepartum haemorrhage and placenta praevia management
exam_tip: In placenta praevia, avoid digital vaginal examination; unstable mother or compromised fetus means emergency escalation and usually caesarean birth.
