tested_concept: Emergency management of severe antepartum haemorrhage with placenta praevia and fetal compromise
learning_objective: Prioritise maternal resuscitation, senior escalation and urgent delivery when antepartum haemorrhage causes maternal instability and fetal compromise.

rationale: Topical NSAIDs are recommended for knee osteoarthritis and have lower systemic adverse-effect risk than oral NSAIDs, making them suitable in a patient with chronic kidney disease and previous peptic ulcer bleeding. Oral diclofenac without gastroprotection is unsafe and increases renal, gastrointestinal and cardiovascular risks. Codeine may be considered only in selected cases and is not preferred initially due to adverse effects and dependence risk. Glucosamine is not recommended as a disease-modifying or analgesic treatment. Regular oral prednisolone is not a standard treatment for osteoarthritis.
clinical_context: UK osteoarthritis care emphasises education, exercise and weight management, with topical NSAIDs commonly used for localised knee or hand symptoms.
simplified_explanation: For knee arthritis pain, an anti-inflammatory gel can help and is safer than anti-inflammatory tablets in someone with kidney disease and ulcer history.
guideline_anchor: NICE osteoarthritis guidance
exam_tip: For knee or hand osteoarthritis, topical NSAIDs are often the first pharmacological choice, especially if oral NSAIDs are risky.
tested_concept: Initial analgesic management of osteoarthritis when oral NSAIDs are higher risk
learning_objective: Choose topical NSAIDs as an appropriate first-line analgesic option for knee osteoarthritis, particularly when systemic NSAID risk is increased.

rationale: The major complication of Kawasaki disease is coronary artery aneurysm or other coronary involvement, assessed with echocardiography. CT brain and EEG are not relevant to the main complication. Lumbar puncture may be considered if meningitis is suspected, but it does not assess Kawasaki complications. Renal ultrasound is not the key investigation.
clinical_context: Children with suspected Kawasaki disease require urgent paediatric assessment, treatment with intravenous immunoglobulin and aspirin when indicated, and cardiac imaging follow-up.
simplified_explanation: Kawasaki disease can damage the coronary arteries, so an ultrasound scan of the heart is needed.
guideline_anchor: NICE and standard UK paediatric practice for Kawasaki disease assessment
exam_tip: Kawasaki disease complication equals coronary artery aneurysm; investigation equals echocardiography.
tested_concept: Use of echocardiography to assess coronary artery involvement in Kawasaki disease
learning_objective: Identify echocardiography as the key investigation for coronary artery complications in suspected Kawasaki disease.

rationale: This patient has vitamin B12 deficiency due to pernicious anaemia and neurological symptoms. The best treatment is intramuscular hydroxocobalamin 1 mg on alternate days until there is no further neurological improvement, followed by maintenance every 2 months. Three-monthly injections without loading doses are used for maintenance in uncomplicated B12 deficiency and are insufficient here. Folic acid alone may worsen neurological complications if B12 deficiency is untreated. Low-dose oral cyanocobalamin is not appropriate for pernicious anaemia with neurological signs. Iron is not the primary deficiency.
clinical_context: In UK practice, suspected pernicious anaemia with neurological features is treated promptly with parenteral B12 and does not wait for specialist review.
simplified_explanation: Low B12 can damage nerves. Because she has numbness, she needs frequent B12 injections at first, then lifelong maintenance injections.
guideline_anchor: BNF and NICE Clinical Knowledge Summaries guidance on anaemia due to vitamin B12 deficiency
exam_tip: Neurological symptoms in B12 deficiency mean alternate-day hydroxocobalamin loading and 2-monthly maintenance.
tested_concept: Prescribing treatment for vitamin B12 deficiency with neurological involvement
learning_objective: Select intramuscular hydroxocobalamin with an appropriate neurological loading regimen for pernicious anaemia causing B12 deficiency.

rationale: Sudden pain, pallor, coldness, absent pulses and neurological signs indicate acute limb ischaemia, likely embolic from atrial fibrillation. Sensory and motor deficits mean the limb is threatened and requires urgent vascular surgery input and immediate intravenous unfractionated heparin unless contraindicated. Imaging may be useful but must not delay senior vascular assessment in a threatened limb. Aspirin alone or delayed outpatient imaging is unsafe. Compression stockings and venous Doppler are for venous disease, not arterial occlusion.
clinical_context: Acute limb ischaemia is a time-critical vascular emergency in UK emergency departments and requires same-day specialist assessment.
simplified_explanation: A blocked artery is starving the leg of blood. Because the nerves are already affected, the leg may be lost unless vascular treatment starts immediately.
guideline_anchor: Vascular Society principles and standard UK emergency vascular practice
exam_tip: Motor or sensory loss in acute limb ischaemia means a threatened limb: call vascular surgery and start IV heparin.
tested_concept: Emergency escalation for acute limb ischaemia with neurological deficit
learning_objective: Recognise threatened acute limb ischaemia and escalate urgently for vascular intervention while starting anticoagulation.

rationale: This patient has symptomatic hypocalcaemia after thyroidectomy, likely due to hypoparathyroidism. Tetany and QT prolongation make this an emergency requiring intravenous calcium gluconate with cardiac monitoring. Oral calcium may be used for mild or maintenance treatment but is too slow here. Zoledronic acid is used for hypercalcaemia, not hypocalcaemia. Salbutamol treats hyperkalaemia or bronchospasm. Treatment should not wait for parathyroid hormone results.
clinical_context: Post-thyroidectomy hypocalcaemia is a recognised complication and symptomatic cases need urgent treatment on an acute surgical or endocrine pathway.
simplified_explanation: Her calcium is dangerously low and affecting muscles and heart rhythm, so calcium must be given directly into a vein while monitoring the heart.
guideline_anchor: BNF and standard UK endocrine emergency practice
exam_tip: Tetany, seizures or prolonged QT with low calcium require IV calcium gluconate.
tested_concept: Emergency treatment of symptomatic severe hypocalcaemia
learning_objective: Treat symptomatic hypocalcaemia with intravenous calcium gluconate and ECG monitoring.

rationale: An adult patient with capacity has the right to confidentiality. The doctor should not disclose diagnosis, investigations or treatment plans to relatives without consent. It is appropriate to encourage the patient to involve trusted family or friends for support, but disclosure cannot be forced unless there is an overriding public interest or serious risk to others, which is not present here. Being next of kin does not automatically grant access to clinical information. Confirming attendance may itself breach confidentiality if the patient has not consented.
clinical_context: Young men with suspected testicular cancer often need sensitive communication about fertility, treatment and family support, while maintaining confidentiality.
simplified_explanation: Even if his mother is worried, the information belongs to the patient. Doctors should support him to share it, but cannot share it for him without permission.
guideline_anchor: GMC confidentiality guidance
exam_tip: Next of kin is not the same as legal permission to receive confidential information.
tested_concept: Confidentiality for an adult patient with suspected testicular cancer
learning_objective: Apply GMC confidentiality principles when relatives request information about an adult patient’s cancer care.

rationale: Sudden unilateral pelvic pain, vomiting, an enlarged ovary and an ovarian cyst are highly suggestive of ovarian torsion. Doppler flow does not exclude torsion because intermittent or partial torsion can preserve arterial flow. Persistent severe pain warrants urgent gynaecology involvement and diagnostic laparoscopy with detorsion and ovarian conservation where feasible. Methotrexate is inappropriate with a confirmed intrauterine pregnancy. Delaying surgery risks ovarian necrosis. The presentation is not typical for pelvic inflammatory disease.
clinical_context: Ovarian torsion is a gynaecological emergency, including in pregnancy, and timely surgery aims to preserve ovarian function.
simplified_explanation: The ovary may be twisting on its blood supply. A scan showing some blood flow does not rule this out, so urgent keyhole surgery is needed.
guideline_anchor: RCOG and standard UK gynaecological emergency practice
exam_tip: Normal Doppler flow does not safely exclude ovarian torsion.
tested_concept: Management of suspected ovarian torsion in pregnancy despite preserved Doppler flow
learning_objective: Escalate suspected ovarian torsion for urgent surgical assessment and laparoscopy rather than relying on Doppler flow to exclude it.

rationale: Autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease is associated with intracranial berry aneurysms. A thunderclap headache with vomiting and meningism is concerning for subarachnoid haemorrhage and requires emergency hospital assessment, including urgent CT brain. Renal ultrasound and antibiotics do not address the life-threatening neurological presentation. Outpatient neurology referral or reassurance is unsafe.
clinical_context: Patients with ADPKD may present outside renal clinics with complications, and clinicians must recognise neurological red flags needing emergency care.
simplified_explanation: People with polycystic kidney disease have a higher risk of brain aneurysms. A sudden severe headache with neck stiffness could be bleeding around the brain.
guideline_anchor: NICE guidance on headaches and standard UK emergency stroke/neurosurgical practice
exam_tip: In ADPKD, thunderclap headache should make you think of ruptured intracranial aneurysm.
tested_concept: Recognition of possible aneurysmal subarachnoid haemorrhage in autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease
learning_objective: Escalate thunderclap headache in a patient with ADPKD for emergency assessment of possible intracranial aneurysm rupture.

rationale: Confirmed gonorrhoea should be treated promptly. In the absence of susceptibility data, ceftriaxone 1 g intramuscularly is recommended. Culture should be obtained where possible to support antimicrobial resistance surveillance, but treatment should not be delayed. Partner notification and test of cure are key parts of management. Doxycycline treats chlamydia rather than gonorrhoea. Azithromycin monotherapy and oral cefixime are not preferred first-line treatment in this setting. Waiting for susceptibility risks ongoing transmission and complications.
clinical_context: UK sexual health services manage gonorrhoea with antimicrobial stewardship, partner notification and follow-up because of resistance concerns.
simplified_explanation: Gonorrhoea needs an injection antibiotic, and contacts need tracing and treating. A follow-up test checks the infection has cleared.
guideline_anchor: BASHH gonorrhoea guideline and UKHSA antimicrobial resistance principles
exam_tip: For gonorrhoea, think ceftriaxone plus partner notification and test of cure.
tested_concept: Management of confirmed gonorrhoea when susceptibility is not yet available
learning_objective: Treat gonorrhoea with recommended ceftriaxone therapy and include culture, partner notification and test of cure.

rationale: A placenta completely covering the internal os at 36 weeks is placenta praevia and vaginal birth is contraindicated because of the risk of severe haemorrhage. Planned caesarean birth is usually arranged at 36 to 37 weeks with senior obstetric, anaesthetic and blood bank planning. Induction, attempted vaginal delivery and awaiting spontaneous labour are unsafe. Repeating ultrasound at 41 weeks delays necessary delivery. External cephalic version is not relevant and may be hazardous.
clinical_context: Placenta praevia is managed in consultant-led obstetric care with delivery planning to minimise maternal and fetal risk.
simplified_explanation: The placenta is blocking the birth canal. Labour could cause heavy bleeding, so a planned caesarean is the safest birth plan.
guideline_anchor: RCOG Green-top guidance on placenta praevia and placenta accreta spectrum, and NICE caesarean birth principles
exam_tip: Placenta covering the os near term means caesarean birth, not induction.
tested_concept: Planned delivery for persistent placenta praevia at term
learning_objective: Select planned caesarean birth at 36-37 weeks for placenta praevia covering the internal cervical os.

rationale: Nephrotic syndrome causes heavy urinary protein loss, leading to hypoalbuminaemia. Albumin normally helps retain fluid within the intravascular space; low albumin reduces plasma oncotic pressure and promotes movement of fluid into tissues, causing oedema. Plasma oncotic pressure is reduced, not increased. Catecholamine excess and lymphatic obstruction are not the primary mechanisms. Nephrotic syndrome usually involves sodium and water retention rather than direct sodium loss.
clinical_context: Children with nephrotic syndrome commonly present to primary care or paediatrics with facial swelling, oedema and heavy proteinuria.
simplified_explanation: Protein leaks out in the urine. With less protein in the blood, fluid moves out into the tissues and causes swelling.
guideline_anchor: Standard UK clinical practice
exam_tip: Nephrotic oedema is mainly about protein loss causing low albumin and low oncotic pressure.
tested_concept: Pathophysiology of oedema in nephrotic syndrome
learning_objective: Explain oedema in nephrotic syndrome as a consequence of heavy proteinuria causing hypoalbuminaemia and reduced oncotic pressure.

rationale: In the nasal polyp group, 60 have asthma and 90 do not. In the control group, 30 have asthma and 120 do not. The odds ratio is (60 × 120) / (90 × 30) = 7200 / 2700 = 2.67, approximately 2.7. This means asthma is associated with higher odds of nasal polyps in this study. The other options result from incorrect use of risks or inverted table values.
clinical_context: Nasal polyps are associated with asthma and aspirin-exacerbated respiratory disease, and epidemiological studies often quantify such associations using odds ratios.
simplified_explanation: For an odds ratio, multiply the diagonal numbers in the 2 by 2 table and divide by the other diagonal: 60 times 120 divided by 90 times 30.
guideline_anchor: Standard UK epidemiology and evidence-based medicine teaching
exam_tip: For case-control studies, use odds ratios rather than relative risks.
tested_concept: Calculating an odds ratio from a case-control study
learning_objective: Calculate and interpret the odds ratio for an exposure-disease association using a 2 by 2 table.

rationale: A large AAA found on screening normally requires urgent vascular referral, but new severe abdominal or back pain with hypotension suggests leaking or rupturing AAA. This is a time-critical emergency requiring 999 transfer to hospital. Routine surveillance, outpatient referral or delayed imaging would be unsafe. Oral analgesia alone does not address the risk of catastrophic haemorrhage.
clinical_context: AAA screening in the UK aims to detect aneurysms before rupture, but symptomatic aneurysms require emergency management rather than the usual screening pathway.
simplified_explanation: A large swollen artery in the abdomen plus sudden severe pain and low blood pressure may mean it is leaking or rupturing. This needs an ambulance immediately.
guideline_anchor: NHS AAA Screening Programme and standard UK emergency practice
exam_tip: Screening pathways apply to stable patients; symptoms of rupture override routine referral timelines.
tested_concept: Emergency escalation when a screening-detected abdominal aortic aneurysm becomes symptomatic
learning_objective: Recognise that sudden abdominal or back pain with hypotension in a patient with a large abdominal aortic aneurysm requires immediate emergency transfer.

rationale: This patient has early alcohol withdrawal. In hospital, symptom-triggered benzodiazepine treatment such as chlordiazepoxide or diazepam, with monitoring and thiamine supplementation, is appropriate. Acamprosate is for relapse prevention after withdrawal, not acute withdrawal. Haloperidol may be used cautiously for severe agitation or hallucinations but does not treat the underlying withdrawal risk. Advising reduction after discharge is unsafe during active withdrawal. Methadone is used for opioid dependence, not alcohol withdrawal.
clinical_context: Hospital admissions are common triggers for alcohol withdrawal because dependent patients abruptly stop drinking while receiving treatment for another condition.
simplified_explanation: Alcohol withdrawal can cause seizures and delirium. Benzodiazepines calm the overactive nervous system, and thiamine helps prevent Wernicke’s encephalopathy.
guideline_anchor: NICE guidance on alcohol-use disorders and BNF prescribing principles
exam_tip: In alcohol withdrawal, think benzodiazepine plus thiamine; relapse-prevention drugs come later.
tested_concept: Management of acute alcohol withdrawal in an inpatient
learning_objective: Select benzodiazepine-based assisted withdrawal and thiamine supplementation for a dependent drinker developing withdrawal symptoms in hospital.

rationale: This is likely immune thrombocytopenia: isolated severe thrombocytopenia, normal coagulation and no features of microangiopathic haemolysis. Symptomatic severe thrombocytopenia warrants treatment, usually corticosteroids after haematology discussion. Platelet transfusion alone is ineffective in ITP and is reserved for life-threatening bleeding alongside other therapy. Plasma exchange is used for suspected thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura, which would usually show schistocytes and haemolysis. Splenectomy is not first-line initial treatment. Observation alone is inappropriate with gum bleeding and platelets of 9 × 10^9/L.
clinical_context: Adults with suspected ITP and significant thrombocytopenia should be assessed for bleeding severity and managed with haematology input.
simplified_explanation: Her immune system is likely destroying platelets. Steroids reduce this immune attack and help the platelet count recover.
guideline_anchor: standard UK haematology practice and BNF corticosteroid principles
exam_tip: Isolated thrombocytopenia with normal clotting suggests ITP; schistocytes would point towards TTP.
tested_concept: Initial management of immune thrombocytopenia with mucosal bleeding
learning_objective: Recognise likely immune thrombocytopenia and select corticosteroid therapy as initial treatment when platelet count is very low with bleeding symptoms.

rationale: Trigeminal neuralgia causes brief, severe, unilateral facial pain in the trigeminal nerve distribution, often triggered by light touch, chewing or toothbrushing. Cluster headache causes longer attacks with autonomic features such as lacrimation and nasal congestion. Glossopharyngeal neuralgia usually affects the throat, tonsillar area or ear and is triggered by swallowing. Migraine lasts hours and is often associated with photophobia, nausea or aura. Temporomandibular joint dysfunction causes jaw pain related to movement, not seconds-long shock-like attacks.
clinical_context: Trigeminal neuralgia commonly presents in primary care as recurrent unilateral facial pain and may be mistaken for dental disease.
simplified_explanation: Short bursts of severe facial pain triggered by light touch are typical of trigeminal neuralgia.
guideline_anchor: NICE Clinical Knowledge Summary on trigeminal neuralgia
exam_tip: Seconds-long, triggerable facial pain with normal examination is classic trigeminal neuralgia.
tested_concept: Recognition of trigeminal neuralgia from brief triggered unilateral facial pain
learning_objective: Diagnose trigeminal neuralgia from paroxysmal electric or stabbing facial pain in a trigeminal distribution with trigger factors and normal examination.

rationale: This patient is likely dying from progressive multi-organ dysfunction in the context of advanced cancer and sepsis. His advance care plan clearly declines hospital admission and intensive care. The appropriate management is individualised end-of-life care, including anticipatory medicines, symptom control and support for the family. Dialysis, CPR, chemotherapy and repeated blood tests would not meet his goals and are unlikely to provide benefit.
clinical_context: Palliative care in the UK emphasises recognising dying, respecting advance care plans and managing distressing symptoms such as pain, breathlessness, agitation and secretions.
simplified_explanation: When the body’s organs are failing at the end of life and the patient has chosen comfort care, treatment should focus on comfort and support rather than burdensome escalation.
guideline_anchor: NICE guidance on care of dying adults in the last days of life
exam_tip: In end-of-life questions, match treatment to the patient’s goals and previously expressed wishes.
tested_concept: Palliative management when multi-organ failure occurs in advanced illness in line with advance care planning
learning_objective: Prioritise comfort, communication and individualised end-of-life care when multi-organ dysfunction occurs in a patient with advanced disease who has declined escalation.

rationale: The fluctuating fatigable ocular and bulbar weakness with normal pupils and reflexes is typical of myasthenia gravis. When acetylcholine receptor and MuSK antibodies are negative, neurophysiology is important; single-fibre EMG is highly sensitive for impaired neuromuscular transmission. CT thorax is used to assess for thymoma after diagnosis but does not confirm MG. MRI brain would investigate central lesions but the pattern is not typical of stroke or demyelination. CK is more useful for myopathy. Oligoclonal bands support multiple sclerosis, not myasthenia gravis.
clinical_context: Patients with suspected myasthenia gravis are usually referred to neurology for antibody testing, neurophysiology and assessment for thymic disease.
simplified_explanation: Myasthenia affects the signal between nerve and muscle. Single-fibre EMG checks whether that signal is failing when muscles are used repeatedly.
guideline_anchor: standard UK neurology practice
exam_tip: In antibody-negative suspected MG, think neurophysiology, especially single-fibre EMG.
tested_concept: Confirming seronegative myasthenia gravis using neurophysiology
learning_objective: Select single-fibre electromyography as a sensitive confirmatory test for suspected myasthenia gravis when antibodies are negative.

rationale: Aspirin 300 mg should be started immediately in suspected TIA unless contraindicated, with urgent specialist assessment. Clopidogrel may be used for longer-term secondary prevention after specialist assessment, but immediate aspirin is the key initial step. Aspirin 75 mg plus dipyridamole is not the recommended immediate regimen. Warfarin is not started empirically unless there is a confirmed indication such as atrial fibrillation and appropriate assessment. Alteplase is for selected patients with acute ischaemic stroke within a time window and persistent deficit, not a resolved TIA.
clinical_context: TIA carries a high early risk of stroke, so UK practice is immediate aspirin and same-day or next-day specialist TIA assessment.
simplified_explanation: A TIA is a warning sign for stroke. A high initial dose of aspirin reduces the chance of another clot while urgent assessment is arranged.
guideline_anchor: NICE guidance on stroke and transient ischaemic attack
exam_tip: For suspected TIA: aspirin 300 mg immediately, then urgent specialist review.
tested_concept: Immediate antiplatelet prescribing for suspected TIA
learning_objective: Prescribe aspirin 300 mg immediately for suspected TIA unless contraindicated, alongside urgent specialist assessment.

rationale: Fever, rigors, loin pain, hypotension and haemoglobinuria shortly after starting red cells suggest an acute haemolytic transfusion reaction, often due to ABO incompatibility. The transfusion must be stopped immediately, IV access maintained with 0.9% sodium chloride, and urgent senior, laboratory and transfusion support obtained. Slowing or restarting the transfusion is unsafe. Furosemide may be relevant in transfusion-associated circulatory overload, but this presentation suggests haemolysis. Antihistamine alone is appropriate only for mild allergic reactions.
clinical_context: Any suspected serious transfusion reaction in UK practice requires stopping the transfusion, checking patient and unit identity, supportive care, and notifying the transfusion laboratory.
simplified_explanation: This looks like the wrong blood may be attacking her red cells. Stop the transfusion immediately and treat it as an emergency.
guideline_anchor: UK transfusion safety practice and Serious Hazards of Transfusion principles
exam_tip: Severe symptoms during transfusion: stop transfusion first, then assess and investigate.
tested_concept: Immediate management of suspected acute haemolytic transfusion reaction
learning_objective: Recognise severe transfusion reaction features and stop the transfusion immediately while maintaining IV access and escalating urgently.

rationale: Pelvi-ureteric junction obstruction can cause intermittent flank pain after a fluid load because urine flow increases and the renal pelvis distends. Ultrasound typically shows hydronephrosis with renal pelvic dilatation but no ureteric dilatation because the obstruction is at the junction of the renal pelvis and ureter. A distal ureteric stone would usually cause hydroureter and often haematuria. Benign prostatic enlargement and urethral stricture cause lower urinary tract obstruction, often bilateral upper tract effects if severe. Vesicoureteric reflux is more typically associated with recurrent urinary infections and childhood presentation.
clinical_context: PUJ obstruction may present in young adults with intermittent hydronephrosis and episodic loin pain, sometimes after alcohol or high fluid intake.
simplified_explanation: The blockage is where the kidney drainage funnel meets the ureter, so the kidney pelvis swells but the ureter below it is not enlarged.
guideline_anchor: standard UK urology practice
exam_tip: Hydronephrosis without hydroureter points to obstruction at or above the pelvi-ureteric junction.
tested_concept: Recognition of pelvi-ureteric junction obstruction causing intermittent hydronephrosis
learning_objective: Identify pelvi-ureteric junction obstruction from intermittent loin pain precipitated by diuresis with renal pelvic dilatation and no hydroureter.

rationale: A pituitary macroadenoma causing bitemporal visual field loss may make driving unsafe, especially for a professional driver. The patient should be advised to stop driving and notify the DVLA. The benign nature of the tumour does not remove the safety issue. Informing only the employer is insufficient. Doctors should normally advise the patient to notify the DVLA first; direct disclosure without consent is considered if the patient continues to drive despite advice and poses a risk to others.
clinical_context: Pituitary tumours can compress the optic chiasm and cause visual field defects relevant to driving entitlement in the UK.
simplified_explanation: His side vision is impaired, so driving could endanger passengers and the public. He must stop driving and tell the DVLA.
guideline_anchor: GMC confidentiality guidance and DVLA medical fitness to drive guidance
exam_tip: For unsafe driving: advise stop driving and DVLA notification first; disclose without consent only if refusal creates public risk.
tested_concept: Driving advice and DVLA notification for pituitary tumour causing visual field impairment
learning_objective: Apply UK driving safety and confidentiality principles by advising a patient with visual field loss to stop driving and notify the DVLA.

rationale: This patient has non-metastatic, locally advanced oropharyngeal squamous cell carcinoma and is fit for curative treatment. If surgery would cause major functional morbidity, definitive radiotherapy with concurrent cisplatin is an appropriate organ-preserving curative approach. Extensive primary surgery may be appropriate in selected cases but is not best here given the MDT assessment. Palliative radiotherapy is for incurable disease or patients unfit for curative treatment. Cetuximab alone is not definitive treatment. Observation would be unsafe for a proven invasive cancer.
clinical_context: In UK practice, head and neck cancers are managed through a specialist MDT considering tumour site, stage, HPV status, fitness, function and patient preference.
simplified_explanation: The cancer has not spread distantly and the patient is fit, so treatment should aim to cure it. Chemotherapy given with radiotherapy can treat the cancer while avoiding very mutilating surgery.
guideline_anchor: NICE head and neck cancer guidance and standard UK head and neck cancer MDT practice
exam_tip: For locally advanced head and neck squamous cancer, think MDT-led curative treatment; concurrent cisplatin chemoradiotherapy is a key organ-preserving option in fit patients.
tested_concept: Definitive concurrent chemoradiotherapy for locally advanced oropharyngeal squamous cell carcinoma when organ-preserving treatment is appropriate
learning_objective: Select concurrent cisplatin-based chemoradiotherapy as an appropriate curative organ-preserving treatment for fit patients with locally advanced head and neck squamous cell cancer.

rationale: Hereditary angioedema causes recurrent, prolonged angioedema without urticaria or itch, often triggered by trauma or dental procedures, and may cause abdominal pain due to bowel wall oedema. A family history supports the diagnosis. IgE-mediated anaphylaxis is acute, usually develops rapidly and commonly includes urticaria, wheeze or hypotension. Chronic spontaneous urticaria involves recurrent itchy wheals. Oral allergy syndrome causes immediate oral itching or mild swelling after raw fruit or vegetables. Serum sickness-like reactions cause fever, rash and arthralgia after drug exposure or infection.
clinical_context: Patients with suspected hereditary angioedema in UK primary care should be referred to an immunology or allergy specialist because standard antihistamines and adrenaline may not control attacks.
simplified_explanation: Repeated swelling without hives or itch, lasting days and running in the family, points to hereditary angioedema rather than a usual allergy.
guideline_anchor: standard UK clinical practice and specialist allergy/immunology guidance
exam_tip: Angioedema without urticaria, especially with abdominal pain and family history, should make you think of hereditary angioedema.
tested_concept: Recognition of hereditary angioedema presenting with recurrent non-urticarial angioedema and abdominal attacks
learning_objective: Differentiate bradykinin-mediated hereditary angioedema from IgE-mediated allergic reactions and urticaria-associated angioedema.

rationale: This transplant recipient is at high risk of severe COVID-19 and is within the treatment window for early antiviral therapy. Nirmatrelvir plus ritonavir has major interactions with calcineurin inhibitors such as tacrolimus, risking serious toxicity, so it is unsuitable without specialist management. A 3-day course of intravenous remdesivir is an appropriate alternative. Dexamethasone is used in COVID-19 patients requiring oxygen, not in non-hypoxic early disease. Azithromycin is not an antiviral treatment for COVID-19. High-risk patients may benefit from antiviral therapy even if not hypoxic.
clinical_context: In the UK, high-risk patients with COVID-19 are assessed through local specialist pathways, with careful checking for renal function and drug interactions before antiviral prescribing.
simplified_explanation: He is high risk and early in the illness, so he should get antiviral treatment. The usual oral option interacts dangerously with tacrolimus, so intravenous remdesivir is a safer choice.
guideline_anchor: NICE COVID-19 rapid guideline and BNF drug interaction principles
exam_tip: Always check ritonavir interactions; tacrolimus and ciclosporin are major red flags.
tested_concept: Selecting antiviral treatment for high-risk non-hospitalised COVID-19 when nirmatrelvir-ritonavir is unsuitable due to major drug interactions
learning_objective: Choose remdesivir as an option for early symptomatic COVID-19 in a high-risk patient when ritonavir-containing treatment is contraindicated or unsuitable.

rationale: The reduction from a crude relative risk of 3.0 to an adjusted hazard ratio of 1.4 suggests that factors such as BMI explain part of the apparent association. Because the 95% confidence interval includes 1, the adjusted association is not statistically significant at the conventional 5% level. A hazard ratio of 1.4 is a relative measure, not a 40% absolute risk. Cohort studies can measure incidence and risk. A non-significant result does not prove there is no relationship; it indicates insufficient evidence of an independent association in this analysis.
clinical_context: PCOS is associated with metabolic risk, but epidemiological interpretation requires distinguishing crude associations from adjusted estimates affected by obesity and other confounders.
simplified_explanation: The initial link looks strong, but once BMI and other factors are considered, the remaining link is smaller and uncertain because the confidence interval includes 1.
guideline_anchor: standard epidemiological principles used in UK clinical practice
exam_tip: If a confidence interval for a ratio measure crosses 1, the result is not statistically significant.
tested_concept: Interpreting confounding and confidence intervals in an epidemiological study of PCOS-related metabolic risk
learning_objective: Interpret how adjustment for confounders affects an observed association and recognise when a confidence interval crossing 1 is not statistically significant.

rationale: This patient has a painful inflamed breast lesion with fever, tachycardia, hypotension and immunosuppression, suggesting infected cyst or breast abscess with sepsis. She needs urgent hospital assessment, sepsis management, intravenous antibiotics and likely imaging-guided aspiration or drainage. Routine breast clinic review, delayed oral antibiotics or reassurance are unsafe. Mammography may be needed later to assess underlying pathology, especially in older women, but immediate management of sepsis takes priority.
clinical_context: Most simple breast cysts are benign and managed in breast clinics, but systemic illness or sepsis requires same-day emergency escalation.
simplified_explanation: This is no longer just a cyst; she is showing signs of a serious infection affecting the whole body, so she needs urgent hospital care.
guideline_anchor: NICE sepsis guidance and standard UK breast surgery practice
exam_tip: A breast lump plus hypotension, fever or immunosuppression is an acute infection problem first, not a routine breast clinic problem.
tested_concept: Emergency escalation for an infected breast cyst or abscess with systemic features of sepsis
learning_objective: Recognise that a painful inflamed breast cyst with systemic instability requires urgent hospital assessment rather than routine outpatient management.

rationale: In women under 40, premature ovarian insufficiency should be considered when menopausal symptoms are associated with infrequent or absent periods. Diagnosis is supported by raised FSH levels on two samples taken 4-6 weeks apart. Anti-Müllerian hormone is not recommended for routine diagnosis. CT, CA125 and endometrial thickness measurement do not diagnose premature ovarian insufficiency and would be guided by other symptoms such as suspected malignancy or abnormal bleeding patterns.
clinical_context: In UK primary care, menopause is usually diagnosed clinically in women over 45, but women under 40 require investigation for premature ovarian insufficiency and assessment of long-term bone and cardiovascular health.
simplified_explanation: Because she is under 40, blood tests are needed. Two raised FSH results several weeks apart support early ovarian failure.
guideline_anchor: NICE menopause guideline
exam_tip: Over 45: diagnose menopause clinically. Under 40: think premature ovarian insufficiency and repeat FSH.
tested_concept: Investigating suspected premature ovarian insufficiency using repeat FSH measurement
learning_objective: Select repeat FSH testing to support a diagnosis of premature ovarian insufficiency in a woman under 40 with menopausal symptoms and oligomenorrhoea.

rationale: The presentation is typical of IgA vasculitis, but this child has significant renal involvement: heavy proteinuria, haematuria, hypertension and raised creatinine. He requires same-day paediatric assessment and discussion with paediatric nephrology. Simple reassurance is inappropriate because renal disease can be serious. NSAIDs should be avoided or used very cautiously when renal involvement is present. Antihistamines and topical steroids do not address systemic vasculitis. IgA vasculitis is not primarily due to thrombocytopenia, and platelet transfusion is not indicated.
clinical_context: Children with IgA vasculitis are often managed supportively, but UK practice emphasises monitoring blood pressure and urine, with urgent escalation for nephritic or nephrotic features.
simplified_explanation: The rash fits IgA vasculitis, but the urine, blood pressure and kidney test suggest kidney inflammation, so he needs urgent specialist assessment.
guideline_anchor: standard UK paediatric practice and renal referral principles
exam_tip: In IgA vasculitis, always check urine and blood pressure; proteinuria, hypertension or impaired renal function changes management.
tested_concept: Management escalation in IgA vasculitis with significant renal involvement and hypertension
learning_objective: Recognise renal red flags in IgA vasculitis and arrange urgent paediatric assessment and specialist renal input.

rationale: This patient has unstable bradycardia with adverse features: hypotension and near-syncope. Complete heart block may not respond to atropine. As atropine has been ineffective, immediate transcutaneous pacing is appropriate while calling for expert help and preparing for transvenous pacing if needed. Adenosine treats some supraventricular tachycardias, not complete heart block. Bisoprolol would worsen bradycardia. Observation alone is unsafe. Amiodarone is used for tachyarrhythmias and can worsen conduction problems.
clinical_context: UK resuscitation algorithms prioritise recognising adverse features in bradycardia, giving atropine initially and escalating promptly to pacing or chronotropic support if ineffective.
simplified_explanation: His heart is too slow and his blood pressure is low. Atropine has not worked, so he needs emergency pacing to maintain circulation.
guideline_anchor: Resus Council UK adult bradycardia algorithm
exam_tip: Unstable bradycardia plus failed atropine equals pacing.
tested_concept: Management of unstable bradycardia not responding to atropine
learning_objective: Escalate symptomatic bradycardia with adverse features to pacing when atropine is ineffective.

rationale: Acute cholecystitis requires analgesia, antibiotics and early surgical assessment for laparoscopic cholecystectomy or drainage if unfit. Intravenous co-amoxiclav provides broad cover for common biliary pathogens and is a typical empirical choice where local guidance supports it. Flucloxacillin mainly targets Gram-positive skin organisms and is inadequate for biliary infection. Nitrofurantoin is for lower urinary tract infection. Doxycycline is not appropriate empirical cover for acute cholecystitis. Aciclovir treats herpes viruses, not bacterial biliary infection.
clinical_context: UK hospitals use local antimicrobial guidelines for biliary sepsis, but co-amoxiclav is a common first-line empirical option in uncomplicated acute cholecystitis when there is no penicillin allergy.
simplified_explanation: An infected gallbladder needs antibiotics that cover gut and biliary bacteria. Co-amoxiclav is the best option listed.
guideline_anchor: BNF and local UK antimicrobial prescribing guidance for biliary infection
exam_tip: Acute cholecystitis needs broad Gram-negative and anaerobic cover, not narrow skin or urinary antibiotics.
tested_concept: Empirical antibiotic prescribing for acute calculous cholecystitis
learning_objective: Select an appropriate broad-spectrum empirical antibiotic regimen for acute cholecystitis, alongside source control planning.

rationale: A perianal abscess requires urgent drainage. In Crohn's disease with a high trans-sphincteric fistula, management should preserve sphincter function; examination under anaesthetic allows drainage and loose seton placement to control sepsis and maintain drainage. Antibiotics alone are inadequate for an abscess. Bedside incision may be insufficient and unsafe for complex disease. Fistulotomy through a high tract risks faecal incontinence. Haemorrhoid treatment is irrelevant.
clinical_context: Complex perianal Crohn's disease in the UK is managed by colorectal surgeons and gastroenterology/IBD teams, often combining surgical drainage or setons with medical therapy.
simplified_explanation: There is a pus collection and a complex tunnel involving the sphincter. It needs urgent drainage, but cutting through the sphincter could cause incontinence, so a seton is used.
guideline_anchor: standard UK colorectal surgery and IBD MDT practice
exam_tip: Perianal abscesses need drainage; high or Crohn's-related fistulas need sphincter-preserving specialist management.
tested_concept: Management of complex perianal Crohn's fistula with abscess
learning_objective: Recognise that perianal abscess associated with a complex Crohn's fistula needs urgent drainage and sphincter-preserving management.

rationale: The patient lacks capacity and has progressive multi-organ failure despite maximal support. Decisions must be made in his best interests, taking account of his previously expressed wishes and clinical prognosis. A senior multidisciplinary discussion with the family should explain that treatment may now be burdensome and non-beneficial, and should plan any withdrawal with anticipatory palliative symptom control. Relatives should be consulted but do not make the final legal decision by voting. Continuing treatment indefinitely because of disagreement may be inappropriate if it is not in the patient's best interests. A DNACPR decision alone does not address ongoing burdensome organ support. Withdrawal should not be done abruptly without careful communication unless there is an immediate clinical necessity.
clinical_context: In UK practice, intensive care and palliative care teams often work together when organ support no longer offers a realistic prospect of recovery.
simplified_explanation: If a patient cannot decide, doctors must decide what is best for that patient, using what the patient would have wanted. Families are involved, but they do not have to choose alone.
guideline_anchor: GMC treatment and care towards the end of life guidance; Mental Capacity Act best interests principles
exam_tip: When capacity is absent, relatives inform best interests decisions; they do not provide consent on behalf of an adult unless they have legal authority.
tested_concept: Best interests decision-making and palliative planning when ongoing organ support is burdensome and non-beneficial
learning_objective: Manage end-stage multi-organ dysfunction by using a structured best interests process, involving those close to the patient, and ensuring symptom control if life-sustaining treatment is withdrawn.

rationale: Morning headaches, daytime somnolence and overnight hypercapnia indicate nocturnal hypoventilation due to respiratory muscle weakness. The appropriate management is specialist assessment and initiation of nocturnal non-invasive ventilation, often alongside airway clearance support. Oxygen alone may worsen carbon dioxide retention because it does not correct hypoventilation. Increasing corticosteroids does not treat established ventilatory failure. Lung transplantation is not the standard management for Duchenne-related nocturnal hypoventilation. Reassurance would miss a treatable complication.
clinical_context: Children and young people with Duchenne muscular dystrophy require planned respiratory surveillance as respiratory muscle weakness progresses.
simplified_explanation: His breathing muscles are too weak during sleep, so he retains carbon dioxide. A night-time ventilator supports breathing; oxygen alone does not solve the problem.
guideline_anchor: standard UK paediatric neuromuscular respiratory practice
exam_tip: In neuromuscular disease, hypercapnia points to hypoventilation: treat with ventilatory support, not oxygen alone.
tested_concept: Management of nocturnal hypoventilation in Duchenne muscular dystrophy
learning_objective: Recognise symptomatic nocturnal hypoventilation in Duchenne muscular dystrophy and select nocturnal non-invasive ventilation rather than oxygen alone.

rationale: Severe placental abruption can release thromboplastin-like tissue factor from damaged decidual and placental tissue into the maternal circulation. This activates coagulation, producing thrombin and consuming fibrinogen and other clotting factors, leading to DIC. Anti-platelet antibodies describe immune thrombocytopenia. Reduced hepatic synthesis is not the main acute mechanism. ADAMTS13 inhibition is associated with thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura. Vitamin K deficiency causes a different pattern and is not the mechanism in acute abruption.
clinical_context: Abruption is an obstetric emergency because it can cause fetal hypoxia, maternal haemorrhage and DIC.
simplified_explanation: When the placenta separates, damaged placental tissue can trigger the clotting system everywhere, using up clotting proteins such as fibrinogen.
guideline_anchor: standard UK obstetric practice
exam_tip: In abruption, falling fibrinogen is a major warning sign for significant haemorrhage and DIC.
tested_concept: Pathophysiology of disseminated intravascular coagulation in placental abruption
learning_objective: Explain how severe placental abruption can trigger consumption coagulopathy through tissue factor release and widespread activation of coagulation.

rationale: Septic arthritis of the hip is an orthopaedic emergency. Staphylococcus aureus is a key pathogen in this age group, so intravenous flucloxacillin is an appropriate empirical choice, adjusted according to local microbiology guidance and culture results. Oral phenoxymethylpenicillin is inadequate for septic arthritis. Azithromycin does not provide appropriate empirical cover. Aciclovir treats herpesvirus infection, not bacterial septic arthritis. Doxycycline is not standard empirical treatment and is generally avoided in younger children unless specifically indicated.
clinical_context: A febrile child who cannot weight bear with a painful hip requires urgent orthopaedic assessment, joint aspiration or washout, and intravenous antibiotics.
simplified_explanation: A hot swollen hip joint in a child can rapidly damage the joint. After samples are taken, give IV antibiotics that cover Staphylococcus aureus.
guideline_anchor: BNF for Children and local paediatric antimicrobial guidance
exam_tip: Do not confuse transient synovitis with septic arthritis: fever, inability to weight bear and high inflammatory markers favour septic arthritis.
tested_concept: Empirical antibiotic treatment for suspected paediatric septic arthritis
learning_objective: Select appropriate empirical intravenous anti-staphylococcal antibiotic therapy for suspected septic arthritis of the hip after cultures are taken.

rationale: This is a stable regular narrow-complex tachycardia, most consistent with supraventricular tachycardia. Initial management is vagal manoeuvres with monitoring. If unsuccessful, adenosine is usually used. Synchronized cardioversion is for patients with adverse features or refractory arrhythmia. Amiodarone is not first-line for uncomplicated stable SVT. Oral bisoprolol and discharge would be inappropriate before termination and assessment. Magnesium is used particularly for torsades de pointes, not typical SVT.
clinical_context: The Resuscitation Council UK tachycardia algorithm separates patients with adverse features from stable patients.
simplified_explanation: He is stable, so try safe manoeuvres that stimulate the vagus nerve to stop the SVT before giving drugs or shocks.
guideline_anchor: Resuscitation Council UK adult tachycardia algorithm
exam_tip: Stable regular narrow-complex tachycardia: vagal manoeuvres first, then adenosine if needed.
tested_concept: Initial management of stable regular narrow-complex tachycardia
learning_objective: Manage haemodynamically stable supraventricular tachycardia initially with vagal manoeuvres before adenosine if needed.

rationale: Albumin:creatinine ratio is the recommended screening test for albuminuria in diabetes and can detect low-level albumin excretion that may not be found on dipstick testing. An early morning sample is preferred where practical. Twenty-four-hour urine calcium does not assess diabetic nephropathy. Renal artery Doppler is not a screening test for diabetic kidney disease. Cystatin C may estimate renal function in selected contexts but does not detect albuminuria. Urine eosinophils are not useful for diabetic nephropathy screening.
clinical_context: UK diabetes reviews include kidney surveillance using eGFR and urine ACR to identify chronic kidney disease early.
simplified_explanation: Kidney damage from diabetes often first shows as tiny amounts of albumin in the urine. ACR detects this better than a dipstick.
guideline_anchor: NICE guidance on chronic kidney disease and diabetes care
exam_tip: A negative urine dipstick does not exclude moderately increased albuminuria; use urine ACR.
tested_concept: Screening for albuminuria in diabetic kidney disease
learning_objective: Use urine albumin:creatinine ratio to detect early diabetic kidney disease, even when dipstick testing is negative.

rationale: Metoclopramide is a dopamine antagonist and can cause acute dystonic reactions, particularly in young people. Oculogyric crisis, torticollis, jaw spasm and tongue protrusion are typical. Serotonin syndrome usually includes serotonergic drug exposure, agitation, hyperreflexia, clonus and autonomic instability. Neuroleptic malignant syndrome develops over longer periods with severe rigidity, fever and raised creatine kinase. A generalised seizure would involve impaired consciousness and rhythmic convulsions. Tetanus is not temporally linked to metoclopramide and would not present so rapidly after the drug.
clinical_context: Drug-induced movement disorders are common iatrogenic presentations in acute care and are usually treated with an anticholinergic such as procyclidine.
simplified_explanation: Metoclopramide can suddenly cause involuntary muscle spasms because it blocks dopamine receptors.
guideline_anchor: BNF adverse effects of dopamine antagonist antiemetics
exam_tip: Oculogyric crisis shortly after metoclopramide or prochlorperazine strongly suggests acute dystonia.
tested_concept: Recognition of metoclopramide-induced acute dystonia
learning_objective: Diagnose an acute dystonic reaction after dopamine antagonist exposure in the emergency department.

rationale: Treponemal tests such as EIA and TPPA often remain positive for life after treated syphilis, so they cannot reliably distinguish old treated infection from reinfection. A quantitative non-treponemal test such as RPR provides a titre that supports assessment of active disease and is used to monitor treatment response. Repeating TPPA adds little. IgG avidity is not standard for routine syphilis staging. HSV PCR and hepatitis B antibody testing do not assess syphilis activity.
clinical_context: Sexual health clinics use both treponemal and non-treponemal tests, with RPR or VDRL titres guiding follow-up after treatment.
simplified_explanation: Old syphilis tests can stay positive forever. The RPR level helps show whether infection is active and whether treatment is working.
guideline_anchor: British Association for Sexual Health and HIV syphilis guidance
exam_tip: Treponemal tests diagnose exposure; non-treponemal titres monitor activity and treatment response.
tested_concept: Use of quantitative non-treponemal titres in suspected syphilis reinfection
learning_objective: Select quantitative RPR or VDRL testing to assess disease activity and monitor response in suspected syphilis reinfection, especially when treponemal tests remain positive from previous infection.

rationale: This patient has sepsis-associated DIC with active bleeding, thrombocytopenia, prolonged clotting times, low fibrinogen and high D-dimer. Management is treatment of the underlying sepsis plus supportive transfusion guided by bleeding and results, including platelets, FFP and cryoprecipitate or fibrinogen replacement when fibrinogen is low. Heparin may be considered in selected predominantly thrombotic DIC but is not the sole treatment for active bleeding. Vitamin K alone does not address consumption coagulopathy. Aspirin would worsen bleeding. Waiting until platelets are below 10 is inappropriate in active bleeding.
clinical_context: DIC is usually secondary to a major trigger such as sepsis, trauma, malignancy or obstetric catastrophe.
simplified_explanation: Her clotting system is overactivated and has used up platelets and fibrinogen, so she bleeds. Treat the infection and replace what has been used up.
guideline_anchor: British Society for Haematology guidance on DIC principles
exam_tip: In DIC, always treat the underlying cause; give blood products when there is bleeding or a high-risk procedure.
tested_concept: Management of bleeding DIC with treatment of the underlying cause and replacement of consumed clotting components
learning_objective: Manage DIC by treating the trigger and supporting haemostasis with blood products when there is clinically significant bleeding.

rationale: Pipe lagging is a classic asbestos exposure. Pleural plaques strongly indicate prior asbestos exposure, and lower-zone reticular shadowing with bibasal crackles supports asbestosis. Coal workers' pneumoconiosis and silicosis more typically cause upper-zone nodular disease related to coal dust or silica exposure. Hypersensitivity pneumonitis is linked to organic antigen exposure and often has episodic symptoms. Sarcoidosis more commonly causes bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy and upper-zone involvement.
clinical_context: Asbestos-related disease may present decades after exposure and includes pleural plaques, asbestosis, lung cancer and mesothelioma.
simplified_explanation: Past asbestos exposure can scar the lower parts of the lungs and cause pleural plaques on imaging.
guideline_anchor: standard UK respiratory and occupational medicine practice
exam_tip: Pleural plaques plus basal fibrosis in a former asbestos worker points to asbestosis.
tested_concept: Recognition of asbestosis from occupational exposure, pleural plaques and lower-zone fibrosis
learning_objective: Diagnose asbestosis in a patient with previous asbestos exposure, progressive dyspnoea, basal crackles and pleural plaques.
